transformer.lead: The Transformer removed recurrence from sequence modelling entirely, replacing it with attention alone. Every position attends to every other in a single parallel operation, so the path between any two tokens is one step rather than $O(n)$ — and training, freed from the sequential dependency of an RNN, finally scaled with the hardware.

blocks.b:
An LSTM reads a sequence one step at a time: the state at position $t$ cannot be computed until position $t-1$ is done. Two consequences follow, and both were binding by 2017.

First, **training cannot be parallelised across the sequence**. GPUs were getting much faster at dense matrix products, and an architecture that serialises over length cannot use that.

Second, the **path length between distant tokens is linear**. Gradient signal between position $1$ and position $n$ passes through $n$ multiplicative steps, and the LSTM gate is a mitigation rather than a cure. Attention had already been bolted onto encoder–decoder RNNs in 2014 to give the decoder direct access to encoder states; the Transformer's wager was that the recurrence around it was no longer earning its place.

Each token is projected into a query, a key and a value. A query is compared against every key by dot product, the scores are normalised, and the output is the correspondingly weighted sum of values:

$$\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

The $\sqrt{d_k}$ divisor is not cosmetic. For queries and keys with independent unit-variance components, $q\cdot k$ has variance $d_k$; at $d_k = 64$ the raw scores are spread wide enough to push the softmax into a regime where one weight is near $1$ and the gradient through the rest is effectively zero. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ restores unit variance and keeps the softmax in its responsive range.

The whole operation is two matrix multiplications and a softmax — no loop over positions.

blocks.h: Multiple heads, and why one is not enough
blocks.b:
A single softmax produces one distribution per query, so one attention layer can only express one notion of relevance at a time. The Transformer runs $h = 8$ attention functions in parallel on $d_k = d_v = d_{\mathrm{model}}/h = 64$-dimensional projections, then concatenates:

$$\mathrm{MultiHead}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_1,\dots,\mathrm{head}_h)W^{O}$$

Because each head works in a subspace of $1/h$ the width, the total cost is roughly that of single-head attention at full width. Heads specialise readily — several in trained models track syntactic dependencies, others resolve coreference — though the tidy interpretations found post hoc should be treated with care.

blocks.h: Position has to be put back
blocks.b:
Attention is permutation-equivariant: shuffle the input and the output shuffles with it. The recurrence that was removed was also what carried order, so order must be re-injected. The paper adds fixed sinusoids to the input embeddings,

$$PE_{(pos,2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right), \qquad PE_{(pos,2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)$$

chosen so that $PE_{pos+k}$ is a fixed linear function of $PE_{pos}$ — relative offsets are linearly recoverable. Learned positional embeddings performed near-identically; the sinusoids were preferred for the hope of extrapolating past the training length, a hope later work found largely unrealised. Position encoding has been an active seam ever since, through relative schemes to RoPE.

Attention is $O(n^2)$ in both time and memory: the score matrix has an entry for every ordered pair of positions. At the paper's sequence lengths this was cheap next to the gain, and it bought a constant path length between any two tokens. At the context lengths of the models that followed it became the dominant cost, and the efficient-attention literature — sparse, low-rank, linear, and eventually the IO-aware exact methods — is the direct descendant of this one line in the complexity table.

Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate

roformer.lead: RoFormer replaced the additive position embedding with a rotation. Query and key vectors are turned in two-dimensional subspaces by an angle proportional to the token's absolute position, so that their dot product depends on position only through the difference of the two positions — relative position falls out of the attention score itself instead of being added to it. It cost no parameters, changed no other part of the architecture, and is now the default in nearly every open decoder-only language model.

blocks.b: The original Transformer adds a position vector to the token embedding once, before the first layer; everything downstream has to keep that information alive through the residual stream. Learned absolute embeddings match the sinusoids inside the trained range — the original paper reports nearly identical results — but they are a lookup table with one row per position seen in training, so position 2049 in a model trained to 2048 has no row at all. Relative schemes fixed the semantics: Shaw's learned relative embeddings, Transformer-XL's decomposition, T5's bucketed scalar bias. But all of them work by editing the attention logits, adding a term indexed by $m-n$ into the expansion of $q_m^{\top}k_n$, which binds position to an explicitly materialised score matrix.

RoPE puts position into the vectors instead. Split a $d$-dimensional query into $d/2$ coordinate pairs and rotate pair $i$, indexed from zero, by an angle $m\theta_i$, where $m$ is the token's absolute position and $\theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d}$. Stacked, those $2\times 2$ rotations form a block-diagonal orthogonal matrix $R_m$, and query and key become $R_m W_q x_m$ and $R_n W_k x_n$. The score then collapses:

$$(R_m q)^{\top}(R_n k) = q^{\top} R_m^{\top} R_n k = q^{\top} R_{n-m} k$$

because rotations are orthogonal and their angles add. Absolute positions go in; only the offset comes out. In code it is elementwise: a multiply by $\cos m\theta$ plus a half-swapped, sign-flipped copy times $\sin m\theta$ — no parameters, no extra matmul.

Three properties follow. The frequencies are geometric, as in the sinusoids: fast pairs turn quickly and resolve adjacent tokens, slow pairs carry coarse position across the whole context. The rotation is applied to $q$ and $k$ inside every attention layer, so position is re-supplied at each depth rather than diluted by dozens of residual additions. Because $R_m$ is orthogonal it leaves the norms of $q$ and $k$ untouched, so the score scale and the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ divisor are unaffected. And RoPE never touches the logit matrix, so it composes with kernelised linear attention and with IO-aware kernels such as FlashAttention that never materialise the scores at all.

The paper also argued a long-term decay property: an Abel-summation bound showing that the inner product's envelope shrinks as $|m-n|$ grows, offered as the desirable prior that distant tokens should interact weakly. The bound constrains an envelope under assumptions about query and key magnitudes, not the score a trained model actually produces; read it as motivation rather than proof. Practice settled the question. RoPE was a drop-in change with no parameter cost and equal or better perplexity, and it was taken up by GPT-NeoX, PaLM, LLaMA and nearly every open decoder-only model since.

blocks.h: Where it breaks past training length
blocks.b: Extrapolation was not solved. Beyond the trained length the slow pairs reach rotation angles never seen in training, and quality degrades sharply rather than gracefully. Every fix reshapes the angles: positional interpolation divides positions by a scale factor so a longer context maps back into the trained angular range, trading fine resolution for coverage and needing only brief fine-tuning; NTK-aware scaling and YaRN stretch the slow dimensions while leaving the fast ones alone; and raising the base from $10^4$ to $10^6$ before long-context training is now routine. ALiBi took the opposite route — no embedding at all, just a fixed linear penalty on distance — which extrapolates better but hard-codes monotone decay.

t5.lead: T5 and BART both answered the same question — how to pretrain a full encoder-decoder Transformer — and T5 pushed the framing furthest by casting every task, including regression and classification, as generating a string from a string. The result was that translation, summarisation, question answering and sentence-similarity scoring all shared one model, one loss and one decoding procedure, with the task specified by a prefix in the input rather than by a new output head.

blocks.b:
BERT gave a strong pretrained encoder, but using it meant bolting a fresh randomly-initialised head onto it for each downstream task: a span-start and span-end classifier for SQuAD, a two-way softmax for entailment, a regression layer for STS-B. Each head had its own initialisation, its own learning-rate sensitivity and its own way of failing, and none of the transfer learning applied to it. Generation was worse served still, since BERT's encoder-only, masked-token objective does not give a left-to-right decoder at all, and GPT's decoder-only stack could generate but read its input with only causal attention.

**The unification claim is that the head is unnecessary if the output is text.** "cola sentence: The course is jumping well" produces "unacceptable"; "stsb sentence1: ... sentence2: ..." produces "3.8", a number emitted as a string to one decimal place. Nothing but the text differs between tasks.

blocks.h: Span corruption and why not token masking
blocks.b:
Both models pretrain by corrupting text and asking the decoder to reconstruct it, which is what makes an encoder-decoder trainable without labels. T5's chosen objective drops contiguous spans — mean length $3$, roughly $15\%$ of tokens — and replaces each with a single sentinel token; the target is the concatenation of the dropped spans, each preceded by its sentinel. Because a span collapses to one input token and appears once in the target, both sequences shrink, and training is markedly cheaper per unit of corruption than reconstructing the whole input.

BART instead ran a wider sweep of corruptions — token deletion, sentence permutation, document rotation, text infilling — and found infilling and sentence shuffling the strongest, which is consistent with T5's independent finding. The convergence matters: two labs searching the space arrived at span-level infilling, and it has been the default corruption for encoder-decoder pretraining since.

blocks.h: The paper is mostly an ablation
blocks.b:
T5's substantive content is a systematic sweep, run at fixed compute, over choices the field had been making by taste: architecture (encoder-decoder against language model against prefix LM), objective, corruption rate, span length, dataset, and fine-tuning strategy. The encoder-decoder with a denoising objective won, and it did so at roughly twice the parameters of a comparable decoder-only model for the same compute; tying the encoder and decoder weights brings the count back down and, notably, cost very little accuracy.

The sweep also produced C4, a cleaned Common Crawl dump of several hundred gigabytes, filtered with heuristics — deduplication, discarding lines without terminal punctuation, dropping pages with boilerplate or offensive-word lists. C4 was released, and became the default pretraining corpus for a large slice of subsequent work, arguably a longer-lived contribution than the architecture.

blocks.h: Relative position and the scale ladder
blocks.b:
T5 replaced sinusoidal and learned absolute positions with a simplified relative scheme: a scalar bias added to the attention logit before the softmax, indexed by a bucketed function of the offset $i-j$, with buckets growing logarithmically so that distant positions share parameters. The bias is shared across layers and learned per head. It is cheaper than the relative schemes of Shaw et al. and Transformer-XL because it adds no vector to the keys, only a scalar to the score, and it extrapolates modestly past the training length because far offsets fall in a common bucket.

The model was trained at five sizes from Small to 11B, and the resulting family made the text-to-text interface concrete for practitioners: mT5, Flan-T5 and the instruction-tuning literature all inherit the format directly, and "prefix the task" is the ancestor of the prompt.

An encoder-decoder pays twice at inference. The full input is encoded, then generation is autoregressive over the output, and both stacks hold their own attention — including cross-attention from every decoder layer back to the encoder states. For a classification task whose answer is one word, this is an absurd amount of machinery to emit "entailment", and the string output forfeits the normalised distribution over the label set that a classifier head gives for free. Constrained decoding or scoring the candidate labels recovers some of that, but not without care.

Decoder-only models at scale later showed that in-context learning could reach comparable task generality with a single stack, which is the direction GPT-3 took. Encoder-decoders persist where the input is long and the output short — summarisation, retrieval-augmented generation — precisely where the asymmetry pays.

BART: Denoising Sequence-to-Sequence Pre-training for Natural Language Generation, Translation, and Comprehension

txl.lead: Transformer-XL restored recurrence to the Transformer, but at the level of segments rather than tokens: the hidden states of the previous segment are cached and attended to, without gradient. To make that legal it had to abandon absolute position encoding, since two segments would otherwise carry identical position vectors, and the relative scheme it introduced outlived the recurrence.

blocks.b:
A vanilla Transformer language model cannot condition on more tokens than its attention window, so a long document is chopped into fixed segments — 512 tokens, say — and each is trained in isolation. Two failures follow. **The first token of a segment has no context at all**, and the model must predict it from nothing; the paper calls this context fragmentation, and it is not a rare edge case, since every segment boundary produces a stretch of tokens with impoverished conditioning.

The second failure is at evaluation. To give every token a full window, the standard procedure slides the segment forward one position at a time and recomputes the entire forward pass for a single new prediction. That is correct and ruinously slow: the cost per token is a whole segment's worth of attention, and nothing is reused between adjacent positions even though the two windows overlap almost completely.

The mechanism is small. For layer $n$ and segment $\tau$, concatenate the previous segment's hidden states, detached from the graph, in front of the current ones:

$\tilde{h}^{n-1}_{\tau} = [\mathrm{SG}(h^{n-1}_{\tau-1}) \circ h^{n-1}_{\tau}]$

where $\mathrm{SG}$ is stop-gradient and $\circ$ concatenation. Queries come from the current segment only; keys and values come from the extended sequence. So each layer can reach one segment back, and because the layers stack, the effective receptive field grows to roughly $N \times L$ tokens for $N$ layers and segment length $L$ — the dependency travels down one layer per segment, as in a diagonally-shifted stack.

Stop-gradient is what makes it affordable: no backpropagation through time, so the memory held for gradients does not grow with the depth of the cache, even though storing the cached states themselves does. At evaluation the cache can be made much longer than at training, and each new segment is one forward pass.

With absolute encodings, position $1$ of segment $\tau$ and position $1$ of segment $\tau-1$ receive the same vector, so a token attending into the cache cannot tell how far back it is looking. The fix is to encode the offset rather than the location. Expanding the query-key logit under absolute encodings gives four terms; Transformer-XL rewrites them as

$A_{i,j} = q_i^{\top} k_j + q_i^{\top} W_{k,R} R_{i-j} + u^{\top} k_j + v^{\top} W_{k,R} R_{i-j}$

where $R_{i-j}$ is a sinusoid of the relative distance, and the two absolute-position query terms are replaced by learned global vectors $u$ and $v$ because a query's own position should not matter once distances are relative. The content-based key projection $W_{k,E}$ and the position-based $W_{k,R}$ are kept separate, which the earlier relative scheme of Shaw et al. did not do.

blocks.h: What it bought, and where it went
blocks.b:
On word-level and character-level language modelling the model set the state of the art of its moment across enwik8, text8, WikiText-103 and One Billion Word — the same architecture winning at both character and word granularity, which is unusual. The paper reports dependencies substantially longer than an LSTM's and longer than a vanilla Transformer's, and evaluation faster by a large factor because the sliding recomputation is gone.

The relative-position formulation is the piece that propagated. XLNet built directly on the same backbone, and the line of thought — that position should enter attention as a function of offset — runs through T5's bucketed scalar bias to RoPE's rotation of queries and keys, which is now near-universal in large decoder-only models.

blocks.h: The limits of a detached cache
blocks.b:
Because the cache is stop-gradiented, nothing in it is ever optimised for the role it plays as context; the model learns to read a memory it never learns to write. The receptive field is also bounded rather than unlimited — it grows with depth, but a fixed number of layers gives a fixed horizon, and information older than that is simply gone. Memory grows linearly with the cached length, so the practical window is a GPU-memory decision.

Subsequent work attacked the ceiling from two directions. Compressive Transformer compressed old memories rather than discarding them; the sparse-attention line — Longformer, BigBird, Reformer — abandoned recurrence and instead made a single very long attention pass affordable, which proved the more durable answer as sequence lengths grew.

refs.t: Transformer-XL: Attentive Language Models Beyond a Fixed-Length Context

xlnet.lead: XLNet set out to get BERT's bidirectional context without BERT's corrupted input, by maximising the likelihood of a sequence under all orderings of its factorisation rather than one. Each token is predicted from a random subset of the others while remaining a genuine autoregressive target, so no artificial mask symbol ever enters the input and the joint distribution over masked positions is not assumed to factorise.

blocks.h: Two defects in masked language modelling
blocks.b:
BERT replaces about $15\%$ of tokens with `[MASK]` and predicts them from the rest. This gives every position a two-sided view, which is why it beat GPT on understanding tasks, but it carries two costs the paper names precisely.

**The pretrain-finetune discrepancy**: `[MASK]` appears in pretraining and never at fine-tuning time, so the model is optimised on inputs from a distribution it will not meet again. BERT's partial mitigation — sometimes substituting a random or the original token — reduces but does not remove the mismatch.

**The independence assumption**: BERT predicts all masked positions in parallel, conditionally independent given the unmasked remainder. In "New York is a city", masking both "New" and "York" means the model scores each without seeing the other, and the strong mutual dependence between them is simply not modelled. Autoregressive factorisation has no such gap, but sees only one side.

Take $\mathcal{Z}_T$, the set of all permutations of the index sequence $1 \dots T$, and maximise

$\max_{\theta} \; \mathbb{E}_{z \sim \mathcal{Z}_T}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log p_{\theta}(x_{z_t} \mid x_{z_{<t}})\right]$

Under a random ordering $z$, predicting $x_{z_t}$ conditions on whatever happened to precede it in that ordering, which in expectation is any subset of the sequence — so a token is seen from both sides across samples, while each individual term remains a proper conditional. The product over $t$ is a valid factorisation of the joint, so the independence assumption disappears.

Crucially the input order is untouched. Permutation is implemented entirely through the attention mask, which is what makes it compatible with positional encodings that describe the original sentence. In practice only the last fraction of each permuted sequence is predicted, since predicting from near-empty context is high-variance and slow to converge.

blocks.h: Why two attention streams are needed
blocks.b:
A standard Transformer state $h_{z_t}$ mixes the token's content and its position, which breaks under permutation: the model must know *which* position it is predicting without being told what is there. If it used the ordinary hidden state, the target would be visible in its own representation.

XLNet therefore runs two streams sharing parameters. The content stream $h$ behaves normally and can see $x_{z_t}$ itself, so it can serve as a key and value for later predictions. The query stream $g$ sees position $z_t$ and the content of $x_{z_{<t}}$, but not $x_{z_t}$, and is what produces the prediction. Both are computed in one pass with two attention masks; at fine-tuning the query stream is discarded and the model is an ordinary Transformer. The scheme is exact but roughly doubles pretraining cost.

XLNet also imports Transformer-XL's segment recurrence and relative encodings, giving it a longer context than BERT, and it was trained on considerably more data. It reported gains over BERT across GLUE, SQuAD, RACE and several classification sets, with the largest margins on tasks involving long documents.

That combination is the difficulty. **The permutation objective was entangled with more data, longer context and different hyperparameters**, and RoBERTa showed shortly afterwards that BERT trained longer, on more data, with dynamic masking and without the next-sentence objective, closed much of the gap. XLNet's own ablation did compare against BERT on identical data and hyperparameters and came out ahead, but the controlled margins were small, RoBERTa closed much of the headline gap without changing the objective, and no later work established a decisive advantage for permutation at matched scale — which, with two-stream attention's cost, is why few followed. Two-stream attention's cost meant few followed; masked and causal objectives remain the two that scaled.

RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach

longformer.lead: Longformer made attention linear in sequence length by computing only a structured subset of the score matrix: a sliding window over local neighbours, plus a handful of positions that attend to everything and are attended by everything. It processes documents of several thousand tokens on ordinary hardware, and unlike most efficient-attention schemes it can be initialised from an existing pretrained checkpoint.

blocks.b:
Self-attention materialises an $n \times n$ score matrix, so memory and time grow as $O(n^2)$. BERT's 512-token limit was a consequence, and it bites hardest on exactly the tasks where context is the point — full-document classification, multi-hop question answering over a supporting corpus, coreference across a long narrative.

The workarounds were all lossy. Truncate the document and discard the tail. Chunk it and process segments independently, which reproduces the context fragmentation Transformer-XL identified. Or run a two-stage retrieve-then-read pipeline, whose recall ceiling is set by a retriever that never sees the question and the passage jointly. Transformer-XL's recurrence helped autoregressive language modelling but is left-to-right by construction, so it does not give the bidirectional encoder that classification and extractive QA want.

The **sliding window** gives each token attention over $w/2$ neighbours on each side, costing $O(n \times w)$. Stacking $\ell$ such layers grows the receptive field to $\ell \times w$, exactly as convolutional stacks do, so the top layer integrates far more than one window even though no single layer does.

**Dilated sliding windows** widen the field without extra cost by leaving gaps of size $d$ between attended positions, giving a reach of $\ell \times d \times w$. The paper uses dilation only in upper layers and only in some heads, so that other heads keep the dense local view that fine-grained tasks need.

**Global attention** is task-specified rather than learned: chosen tokens attend to the whole sequence and are attended by it. For classification that is `[CLS]`; for question answering, every token of the question. A small number of such tokens keeps the cost linear while restoring the ability to aggregate globally, which pure local attention cannot do. Global attention uses its own projection matrices, initialised from the sliding-window ones.

The design's practical advantage is that it is a drop-in replacement for the attention operation, leaving the rest of the architecture and the parameter shapes untouched. Longformer starts from RoBERTa's weights, copies the 512 learned position embeddings repeatedly to cover 4096 positions — a crude initialisation, but one that preserves the local structure RoBERTa learned, since within any 512-token stretch the relative offsets are unchanged — and continues pretraining briefly on long documents.

The implementation needed a custom CUDA kernel written in TVM for the banded matrix multiplication, because a naive dense computation followed by masking saves nothing. That detail matters more generally: **a sparsity pattern only pays if the hardware can exploit it**, and banded structure is chosen partly because it maps onto contiguous memory.

blocks.h: What it delivered and what it did not
blocks.b:
Longformer improved on RoBERTa across long-document tasks — WikiHop, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, IMDB, Hyperpartisan — with the gains concentrated where documents genuinely exceed 512 tokens, and it was extended to an encoder-decoder, LED, for long-input summarisation on arXiv-length papers. BigBird arrived close behind with a similar window plus random plus global mixture and a proof of Turing completeness for the pattern.

The unresolved part is that **the sparsity pattern is a prior, hand-designed and fixed**. Which tokens deserve global attention is decided by the task designer, not learned, and a dependency that the window and the global set both miss cannot be represented at all. Later work went two ways: learn the pattern, as in Reformer's hashing and the routing-attention line; or keep attention exactly dense and make it fit in memory by reordering the computation, which is what FlashAttention did — and which, by removing much of the pressure, ended the sparse-attention era rather than improving on it.

Big Bird: Transformers for Longer Sequences

performer.lead: Linformer and Performer both removed the $n \times n$ attention matrix, but by different arguments: Linformer projects keys and values down to a fixed length on the grounds that attention is empirically near low-rank, while Performer rewrites the softmax as a kernel and reassociates the products so the sequence dimension is contracted first. Both reach $O(n)$ time and memory, and both trade exactness for it.

blocks.h: Why the matrix is the cost
blocks.b:
Attention computes $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d})V$ with $Q, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$. The inner product $QK^{\top}$ is $n \times n$, so it costs $O(n^2 d)$ to form and $O(n^2)$ to store — and it must be stored, because the backward pass needs it. At $d = 64$ and $n = 4096$ the score matrix dwarfs the parameters of the layer.

The obstruction to a cheaper computation is precisely the softmax. Without it, $Q(K^{\top}V)$ would contract the sequence dimension first and cost $O(n d^2)$, linear in $n$. The nonlinearity sits between the two matrix products and forbids the reassociation, and every linear-attention method is in some sense an attempt to get around that one placement.

Linformer's starting observation is empirical: the spectrum of the attention matrix in trained Transformers decays fast, with most of the energy in the leading singular values, and the paper argues via the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma that a low-rank approximation is bounded in error.

The mechanism is two learned linear projections $E, F \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times n}$ applied along the sequence dimension of the keys and values before attention:

$\mathrm{head} = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q(EK)^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)(FV)$

The score matrix is now $n \times k$ with $k$ fixed — the paper uses $k = 256$ independent of $n$ — so cost is $O(nk)$. Projections can be shared across heads and layers to save parameters.

The binding constraint is that $E$ and $F$ have $n$ as an input dimension, so **the model is tied to a fixed maximum sequence length** and cannot be applied causally without leaking future information into the projection. Linformer is an encoder method.

Performer keeps the sequence length free by attacking the softmax algebraically. Write the unnormalised attention weight as a kernel, $\exp(q^{\top}k/\sqrt{d}) = \mathbb{E}[\phi(q)^{\top}\phi(k)]$, for a randomised feature map $\phi$. Substituting the estimate $\hat{A} = \phi(Q)\phi(K)^{\top}$ makes the product associative again:

$\phi(Q)\left(\phi(K)^{\top}V\right)$

costs $O(n r d)$ for $r$ random features, never forming anything $n \times n$.

The technical contribution is the choice of $\phi$. Trigonometric random features, the standard construction for a Gaussian kernel, can produce negative estimates of a quantity that is strictly positive, and dividing by a near-zero normaliser then explodes the variance. FAVOR+ uses **positive orthogonal random features** — exponentials rather than sinusoids, so every estimate is positive, and orthogonal rather than i.i.d. random directions, which reduces variance further. The estimator is unbiased with concentration guarantees, and the method applies causally via a prefix-sum, so it works for decoders as well.

Both were evaluated favourably on their own benchmarks, and Performer showed it could approximate a pretrained Transformer closely enough that fine-tuning recovers most of the loss. But Long Range Arena, run across the family of efficient attentions, found the accuracy-speed frontier muddier than individual papers suggested, and reported quality shortfalls against dense attention that varied unpredictably by task. Linear attention consistently underperforms softmax attention on language modelling at scale, a gap usually attributed to the softmax's sharpness — a low-rank or feature-map approximation smooths the distribution and loses the near-one-hot retrieval that induction-head-like behaviours depend on.

The decisive turn was practical rather than mathematical. FlashAttention showed the $n^2$ matrix need never be materialised at all: tile the computation, recompute in the backward pass, and keep the result numerically exact while making memory linear. Given exactness at comparable speed, approximation lost its constituency. The kernel idea survives, though — in state-space and linear-recurrent models such as Mamba and RWKV, where a linear-attention-like recurrence is the point rather than a compromise.

roberta.lead: RoBERTa changes nothing about BERT's architecture: the same encoder, the same masked-language-modelling objective, a different training recipe. Trained on ten times the text, for far longer, with much larger batches and without the next-sentence-prediction loss, it matched or beat every model published against BERT in the intervening year. Its real contribution was the uncomfortable finding that BERT had been badly undertrained, and that the field had been crediting to architecture what belonged to compute.

blocks.b:
In the year after BERT, a run of models — XLNet among them — reported gains and attributed them to new pretraining objectives. Each had also changed the corpus, the batch size and the number of steps, so no published comparison isolated the objective from the budget.

The authors re-ran BERT's own design under a controlled sweep and found the baseline had a great deal of headroom left: it was nowhere near converged at the original budget, and most of the reported gap closed once compute was matched. **Nothing about the encoder needed to change.** The lesson outlived the models involved. A pretraining result reported without a matched-compute baseline says very little, and the discipline of holding the budget fixed while varying one thing became standard practice largely because of this paper.

blocks.h: Dynamic masking, and the loss that went
blocks.b:
BERT chose its masks once, during preprocessing, duplicating the corpus ten ways so each sequence was seen under ten patterns — still four repeats each across forty epochs. RoBERTa samples the mask when the sequence is fed, so no pattern recurs. The gain is small and costs nothing.

Next-sentence prediction was removed outright, on evidence. Dropping the loss and drawing each sequence from a single document matched or beat the original; dropping it and packing full sentences across document boundaries cost nothing downstream either, and is what the final recipe used. NSP's negative half paired sentences from different documents, so the task was largely topic detection, which masked-language modelling already teaches, rather than any model of coherence.

The corpus grew from BookCorpus and Wikipedia, about 16GB, to roughly 160GB with the addition of news, web text and story-style crawl. Batches went from 256 sequences to 8K with the learning rate retuned; large batches improved both perplexity and end-task accuracy while parallelising more cleanly. Training ran to 500K steps and accuracy was still climbing when it stopped.

The tokeniser was swapped for a byte-level BPE of 50K units, which never emits an unknown token — paid for with a larger embedding table and a slight downstream loss the authors accepted for the generality. The result was 88.5 on the GLUE leaderboard, with state-of-the-art numbers on SQuAD and RACE from a model nobody had redesigned.

RoBERTa buys accuracy with compute and leaves every structural inefficiency of BERT standing. The objective still supervises only the masked 15% of positions, so most of the forward pass yields no gradient of its own — the target ELECTRA went after. Parameters are still untied across layers and the embedding matrix still scales with model width, which ALBERT attacked. Inference cost is unchanged, which is DistilBERT's opening. Position is still summed into content at the input, which DeBERTa argued conflates two different things.

It also remains a bidirectional encoder: fine-tuned per task, unable to generate. Within two years the scaling programme it validated had moved to decoder-only models, where the same undertraining lesson reappeared as Chinchilla.

refs.t: RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach

albert.lead: ALBERT keeps BERT's architecture and attacks its parameter count from two directions: a factorised embedding matrix, and one set of layer weights shared by every layer. ALBERT-large carries about 18M parameters against BERT-large's 334M, and the largest configuration set the state of the art on GLUE, SQuAD 2.0 and RACE. The catch, stated plainly in the paper, is that fewer parameters is not less computation.

blocks.b:
BERT-large's 334M split across two pools that behave quite differently. The embedding matrix is $V \times H$ — vocabulary by hidden width — and is only ever looked up, so it is a memory cost carrying no depth. The encoder is $L$ copies of one block shape, each with private weights.

ALBERT's argument for the first is that the embedding is context-independent by construction while hidden states are context-dependent; tying $E = H$ is an implementation accident, and it means every increase in width drags the whole vocabulary table along. The argument for the second is empirical: the weights of successive Transformer layers were observed to be similar to one another, so forcing them to be identical costs less than intuition suggests.

Factorisation inserts a bottleneck. The vocabulary is projected into $E$ dimensions and then up into $H$, so the cost falls from $O(V \times H)$ to $O(V \times E + E \times H)$, a large saving whenever $E \ll H$.

Sharing goes further: one attention block and one feed-forward block, reused at every depth. The paper separates sharing attention only, feed-forward only, and both; both is the default, and most of the degradation comes from the feed-forward half. Together these let ALBERT-xxlarge run at $H = 4096$ with 12 layers and 235M parameters — wider than BERT-large and still smaller. Sharing also regularises: the authors removed dropout entirely and gained again.

ALBERT keeps a sentence-level loss but changes what it asks. NSP drew its negatives from a different document, so topic mismatch gave the answer away and the task collapsed into topic prediction — something masked-language modelling already supplies.

SOP takes two consecutive segments from the same document and, for the negative, swaps their order. Topic is held constant, so the only usable signal is discourse coherence. The asymmetry the argument rests on is measured: a model trained on NSP performs near chance on SOP, while a model trained on SOP does reasonably on NSP. Ablations put a consistent gain on the multi-sentence tasks, RACE in particular. It is a clean example of diagnosing why an auxiliary loss is not earning its place before replacing it.

The saving is in memory and in gradient communication, not in FLOPs. A shared layer is still executed once per depth, and ALBERT-xxlarge — much wider than BERT-large — is slower per step and at inference despite the smaller footprint.

That bounds where the design pays: it helps when the model must fit somewhere, or when data-parallel synchronisation dominates, and it does nothing for latency. The subsequent scaling effort went the other way, towards more parameters, sparsely activated where possible, so cross-layer sharing survives mainly in recurrent-depth and looped-transformer work rather than mainstream encoders. Deployment compression went instead to distillation, pruning and quantisation, which reduce arithmetic as well as storage.

refs.t: ALBERT: A Lite BERT for Self-supervised Learning of Language Representations

distilbert.lead: DistilBERT is BERT-base with half the layers, trained during pretraining rather than after it to reproduce its teacher's output distribution. It keeps 97% of BERT-base's GLUE score at 66M parameters against 110M and runs about 60% faster. It made a fine-tuned Transformer cheap enough to serve routinely, and the checkpoint did more for the practice of distillation than the paper's numbers did.

blocks.b:
Earlier distillation of BERT was task-specific: fine-tune the teacher on a task, then train a small student on that task's data against the teacher's logits. Every new task means another distillation run and another student.

DistilBERT moves the operation upstream. The student is distilled against the teacher's masked-language-modelling distribution over a general corpus, producing a general-purpose checkpoint that is afterwards fine-tuned exactly like any other BERT. That is what made it usable — one artefact, dropped into an existing pipeline, no change of workflow. The cost is that a general student cannot exploit the structure of any particular task, so a task-specific distillation at the same size will usually beat it where someone is willing to run one.

Training minimises a sum of three terms. The distillation loss is a cross-entropy against the teacher's softmax at temperature $T$,

$p_i = \frac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j/T)}$

applied to both networks during training and set back to $T = 1$ at inference. Raising $T$ flattens the distribution and exposes the mass the teacher puts on wrong answers — which token was the second-best guess, and by how much — a far richer target than a one-hot label.

The ordinary masked-language-modelling loss against the true tokens is kept, and a cosine embedding loss aligns the direction of the student's hidden states with the teacher's, pushing the two to represent alike rather than merely to agree at the output.

blocks.h: Where the size was taken from
blocks.b:
The student halves depth, twelve layers to six, and keeps the width at 768. Depth was cut rather than width because latency on the target hardware tracks the number of sequential layers, whereas width mostly changes the size of matrix products the accelerator is already efficient at.

Because the shapes still match, the student can be initialised from every second layer of the teacher, which matters more than it sounds — a randomly initialised student of this size trains markedly worse. Token-type embeddings and the pooler are dropped. Training follows the RoBERTa recipe: large batches, dynamic masking, no next-sentence prediction, on the teacher's corpus.

The headline is an average over GLUE, and GLUE averages flatter small models: several of its tasks have small test sets and sit near saturation. The losses concentrate where depth is doing work — extractive question answering and anything needing multi-step composition show a wider gap than the average implies.

DistilBERT also inherits quadratic attention, so it is smaller but not asymptotically cheaper on long inputs. Later work pressed both seams: TinyBERT and MobileBERT distil intermediate attention maps and hidden states layer by layer — TinyBERT pairing a general stage with a task-specific one, MobileBERT staying deliberately task-agnostic — while structured pruning and quantisation attack the same budget differently. The durable lesson is distributional — a compressed checkpoint people can download beats a better one they must reproduce.

refs.t: DistilBERT, a distilled version of BERT: smaller, faster, cheaper and lighter
Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network

electra.lead: ELECTRA replaces masked-language modelling with a discrimination task: a small generator fills in the masked positions, and the model actually being trained decides, at every token in the sequence, whether it is original or a replacement. The loss is defined over all positions rather than the masked 15%, and the compute-to-accuracy curve moves accordingly — ELECTRA-small trains on one GPU in a few days and beats GPT on GLUE.

blocks.h: The 15% that teach, and the mismatch
blocks.b:
BERT corrupts about 15% of positions and computes a loss only there. The encoder processes the whole sequence, so roughly six-sevenths of every forward and backward pass builds representation but contributes no gradient of its own. Raising the mask rate does not rescue this: mask too much and the context needed for reconstruction is gone.

There is a second, subtler defect. `[MASK]` appears in every pretraining batch and never at fine-tuning, so the network is asked downstream to operate on an input distribution it was not trained on. BERT's rule of sometimes leaving the token and sometimes substituting a random one is a patch on precisely this, and is acknowledged as one.

A small masked-language model, the generator, is trained normally and used to sample plausible tokens at the masked positions. Its samples are spliced back into the sequence, and the discriminator — the model that is kept — is trained with a binary cross-entropy at every position: original, or replaced.

Because the substitutions are plausible rather than random, the task is not trivial; telling "the chef cooked the meal" from "the chef ate the meal" needs the knowledge masked prediction needs. The two train jointly,

$\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MLM}} + \lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{disc}}$

with $\lambda = 50$, because a per-token binary loss is far smaller in magnitude than a vocabulary-sized softmax. The generator is then discarded. The discriminator has never seen `[MASK]`.

The arrangement looks adversarial and the paper is explicit that it is not: the generator is trained by maximum likelihood on the true tokens, not to fool the discriminator.

They tried the adversarial version. Sampling tokens is discrete, so the generator must be trained by reinforcement learning, and it did worse — policy-gradient estimates over a vocabulary-sized action space are poor, and the resulting generator collapsed towards low entropy, which makes detection too easy. Generator capacity matters for the same reason, in both directions: the best setting is a generator between a quarter and a half of the discriminator's width. Too strong, and the replacements become genuinely indistinguishable. Embeddings are shared between the two networks; nothing else is.

blocks.h: What it bought, and what it foreclosed
blocks.b:
At matched compute ELECTRA dominated the encoders of its generation: the base-sized model outperformed BERT-large on GLUE, and the large one matched RoBERTa and XLNet for a fraction of the pretraining cost.

But the objective yields a discriminator, not a generative model. There is no head assigning probability to text, so it cannot generate, cannot be prompted, and cannot do the zero- and few-shot tasks that GPT-3 pushed to the centre of the field within months of publication. As scaling moved to decoder-only next-token prediction, the efficiency argument stopped applying to the models people were building. It survives inside DeBERTaV3, which pairs replaced-token detection with disentangled attention and had to cut the discriminator's gradient out of the shared embedding table, because the two objectives otherwise pull it in opposite directions.

refs.t: ELECTRA: Pre-training Text Encoders as Discriminators Rather Than Generators

deberta.lead: DeBERTa's argument is that BERT discards structure at the input: it adds a position vector to a content vector and asks attention to disentangle them again. DeBERTa keeps the two apart, computing attention from separate content-to-content, content-to-position and position-to-content terms over relative distances, and re-injects absolute position only at the output. An ensemble of its 1.5B-parameter version was the first to pass the human baseline on SuperGLUE.

blocks.b:
In BERT a token's input is the sum of a token embedding and a position embedding. The attention score between positions $i$ and $j$ then expands into four products — content with content, content with position, position with content, position with position — but they are entangled in one vector and share one pair of projections.

The pattern a word induces genuinely depends on both what it is and where it sits relative to its neighbour: "deep" attends to "learning" quite differently when adjacent than when ten tokens away. Forcing one vector to carry both makes the model recover a distinction it was never handed. Relative schemes existed in Transformer-XL and T5; DeBERTa's move is to hold the streams separate through the attention computation itself.

Each token gets two vectors: content $H$ and relative position $P$. The position-to-position term is dropped, since it carries nothing once positions are relative, leaving three — schematically, and suppressing the separate projections each term uses,

$A_{i,j} = H_i H_j^{\top} + H_i P_{j|i}^{\top} + P_{i|j} H_j^{\top}$

where $P_{j|i}$ embeds the relative distance from $i$ to $j$, clipped at a maximum $k$. The first term is ordinary content attention, the second lets content select for an offset, the third lets an offset select for content.

Because three terms are summed rather than one, the scaling becomes $1/\sqrt{3d}$ rather than $1/\sqrt{d}$ — the same variance argument that motivated the original divisor. Relative embeddings are shared across layers, so the parameter cost is small. The compute is not free.

blocks.h: Why absolute position returns at the end
blocks.b:
Relative position alone cannot always settle a masked token. In "a new store opened beside the new mall", predicting the masked "store" requires knowing it is the syntactic subject, and the local relative pattern around it is nearly identical to the one around "mall".

The enhanced mask decoder therefore supplies absolute positions just before the softmax of the masked-language-modelling head, after the encoder stack rather than at its input. The ordering carries the argument: relative position shapes attention at every layer, absolute position informs only the final prediction, so the representations are never tempted to lean on absolute offsets. Ablations attribute a measurable share of the MNLI gain to this component by itself.

blocks.h: Results, cost, and what came after
blocks.b:
DeBERTa-large beat RoBERTa-large on MNLI, SQuAD 2.0 and RACE while pretraining on roughly half as much text — the clearest evidence in this family that inductive bias still bought something once the RoBERTa recipe had absorbed the easy gains. The price is heavier attention: two additional score matrices and a gather over relative offsets at every layer.

The 1.5B model added scale-invariant fine-tuning, an adversarial perturbation applied to normalised word embeddings. DeBERTaV3 then swapped masked-language modelling for ELECTRA's replaced-token detection and fixed the embedding tug-of-war that pairing caused; that checkpoint remains a common default for classification and NLI-based zero-shot pipelines, long after decoder-only models took generation.

refs.t: DeBERTa: Decoding-enhanced BERT with Disentangled Attention

gpt1.lead: GPT-1 showed that a single decoder-only Transformer, pretrained to predict the next token on plain books and then fine-tuned with almost no change of shape, could beat purpose-built models across most of a twelve-task benchmark suite. What transferred was the whole network rather than a table of embeddings, and that is what separated it from word2vec and from ELMo's frozen features.

blocks.b:
Static embeddings gave one vector per word type, so everything above the first layer of a task model was still trained from scratch on whatever labelled data existed. ELMo improved on this by taking contextual states from a bidirectional LSTM language model, but kept them frozen and fed them into an architecture that still had to be designed per task. ULMFiT fine-tuned a recurrent LM end to end, though for classification.

The binding constraint was labelled data. Entailment, semantic similarity, commonsense reasoning and question answering each had their own bespoke encoder, its own inductive biases, and a few thousand examples to fit them with. **Transfer stopped at the word level**, and the expensive part of the model was rebuilt every time.

blocks.h: Two stages, and an auxiliary loss
blocks.b:
Stage one maximises the ordinary autoregressive likelihood over a large unlabelled corpus,

$L_1 = \sum_i \log P(u_i \mid u_{i-k},\dots,u_{i-1};\Theta)$

with a 12-layer masked-self-attention Transformer. The corpus choice mattered: BooksCorpus, roughly seven thousand unpublished books, was preferred over shuffled-sentence benchmarks because contiguous long passages let the model learn dependencies longer than a sentence.

Stage two adds one linear layer on the final token's activation and fine-tunes every parameter. The paper keeps the language-modelling term as an auxiliary objective during fine-tuning, optimising $L_2 + \lambda L_1$, reporting faster convergence and better generalisation — an early observation that the pretraining objective is a regulariser, not merely an initialiser.

Structured tasks look nothing alike: entailment is an ordered pair, similarity is an unordered pair, multiple choice is a context with several candidate answers. The usual answer was a different architecture for each.

GPT-1 instead serialises each into one token sequence using learned delimiter tokens — premise, delimiter, hypothesis — so the pretrained stack sees the only format it knows. Similarity, having no natural order, is processed in both orderings and the representations summed. Multiple choice scores each candidate independently and normalises across them.

The only genuinely new parameters are the delimiter embeddings and one output matrix. This is the germ of the idea that later removes the head altogether: if a task can be written as a sequence, a sequence model can do it.

Two limits. The model is unidirectional, so the representation of a token carries nothing from its right context — a real handicap for classification and span extraction, and precisely the opening BERT walked through months later with masked-token recovery, taking GLUE by a wide margin.

Second, every task still needed labelled examples, its own output head, and its own fine-tuned copy of all the weights. Deployment meant one model per task.

The paper does note that zero-shot behaviour on several tasks improves steadily over the course of pretraining, with no fine-tuning at all. GPT-2 pursued exactly that observation, dropping both the head and the fine-tuning by writing the task in text; GPT-3 then showed that at a hundred times the scale a handful of in-context examples recovers much of what fine-tuning had provided.

refs.t: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training
Deep Contextualized Word Representations (ELMo)

gpt2.lead: GPT-2 left GPT-1's architecture nearly untouched and scaled it to 1.5B parameters over 40GB of quality-filtered web text, then evaluated it on tasks it had never been fine-tuned for by simply describing them in the input. It reached state of the art on seven of eight language-modelling datasets without seeing their training sets, and argued that supervised NLP tasks are a subset of what a language model already has to model.

blocks.h: A task is a conditioning variable
blocks.b:
A supervised system learns $p(\text{output} \mid \text{input})$ for one task. The paper's reframing is that a general system must learn $p(\text{output} \mid \text{input}, \text{task})$, and that on a large enough web corpus the task specification is itself just text — translation pairs, question-and-answer pairs and "in summary" passages occur naturally in documents.

Earlier multitask work had unified tasks under a single format, most notably by casting ten of them as question answering, but still trained on labelled examples of each. **GPT-2 performs no gradient update at test time.** Task specification is a prefix: "TL;DR:" for summarisation, a few example pairs for translation. Prompting, in its crude original form, starts here.

Common Crawl was rejected as largely unintelligible. The authors instead scraped outbound links from Reddit submissions with at least three karma as a cheap proxy for a human having found the page worth sharing: roughly eight million documents, 40GB of text after de-duplication, with Wikipedia removed because so many evaluation sets are built from it.

The tokenizer is byte-level BPE, so no input is ever out of vocabulary, with merges forbidden across character categories to stop the vocabulary spending slots on variants of a word differing only by trailing punctuation. Architecturally the changes are small and stabilising: layer normalisation moved to the input of each sub-block with an extra one after the final block, and residual-path weights scaled by $1/\sqrt{N}$ at initialisation.

blocks.h: Where zero-shot worked and where it did not
blocks.b:
It worked where the task sits close to language modelling. LAMBADA, which requires resolving a long-range dependency to predict a final word, went from a previous best of 59.2% accuracy to 63.2%, with perplexity dropping from 99.8 to 8.6. Reading comprehension on CoQA reached the region of published supervised baselines without any of their training pairs.

It did not work elsewhere. Summarisation barely improved on selecting a few leading sentences. Translation and closed-book factual questions were poor in absolute terms, if remarkable relative to zero.

The more consequential result was a slope rather than a level: with four model sizes trained identically, performance rose log-linearly with capacity on essentially every task, and even the largest model still underfit WebText. The obvious next experiment was to make it much bigger.

Zero-shot numbers remained far below fine-tuned systems on most benchmarks, and were unstable under rewording of the prompt — a sensitivity the field spent years papering over. Likelihood-maximising decoding degenerated into repetition loops, which is the problem nucleus sampling was introduced to fix.

Nothing in the training made the model helpful or truthful; it made it a good imitator of internet text, which is a different thing.

The 1.5B model was withheld at publication over misuse concerns and released some months later, the first time model capability was publicly treated as a release decision rather than a publication detail. GPT-3 answered the level question with roughly another hundredfold of scale and a formalised few-shot prompt.

refs.t: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners

gpt3.lead: GPT-3 scaled the GPT-2 recipe by more than a hundred times, to 175B parameters, and reported that at that size a frozen model can take up a new task from a handful of examples placed in its prompt, with no gradient update at all. In-context learning was not designed in; it was observed, and the paper's central evidence is that it strengthens smoothly and predictably with scale.

blocks.b:
After BERT and GPT-2, using a model still meant assembling thousands of labelled examples per task and producing a separate set of weights to serve. The paper raises three objections. Practically, data collection dominates the cost of every new application. Scientifically, strong fine-tuned scores on a narrow benchmark may overstate ability, because a high-capacity model can exploit spurious regularities in a narrow distribution. And by comparison with people, who generally need an instruction and one or two examples.

The timing was not accidental. Scaling laws published earlier the same year had made test loss a predictable power law in parameters, data and compute, which turned a run of that size from a gamble into an extrapolation with error bars.

96 layers, $d_{\mathrm{model}} = 12288$, 96 attention heads of width 128, a 2048-token context, and dense and locally banded sparse attention layers alternating through the depth. Eight models from 125M upwards were trained under the same recipe so that the trend, not just the endpoint, could be read.

The data is filtered Common Crawl — kept by a classifier trained to recognise text resembling known-good reference corpora, then fuzzily de-duplicated — mixed with a WebText-like set, two book corpora and English Wikipedia. Roughly 300B tokens are sampled, weighted so the small high-quality sets are seen several times and Common Crawl less than once. A flaw in de-duplication against evaluation sets was found after training and analysed in the paper rather than fixed.

At evaluation the prompt holds a natural-language description of the task, then $K$ demonstrations — as many as the 2048-token window allows — then the query, and the model completes it. The weights never move; whatever adaptation occurs happens within a single forward pass.

Few-shot beats one-shot beats zero-shot, and the gaps widen with model size, which the authors read as larger models being better at inferring from context what is being asked. LAMBADA rises to the mid-eighties in accuracy; closed-book TriviaQA is competitive with fine-tuned open-domain systems that retrieve documents. Arithmetic is the most diagnostic result: two-digit addition is close to perfect, and accuracy collapses by five digits, which looks like neither pure memorisation nor a learned algorithm.

The paper's own limitations section lists loss of coherence and self-repetition over long passages, and weakness on tasks that compare two sentences — natural language inference, word-sense-in-context — where the absence of bidirectional context plausibly bites.

Two other gaps drove the next several years. The objective rewards likely text, not helpful or truthful text, so the model will complete a false premise as readily as a true one and answer a question with more questions; that is what InstructGPT set out to fix. And 175B dense parameters are touched for every generated token, making inference the dominant cost and motivating distillation, quantisation and mixture-of-experts routing. Chinchilla later showed this run was badly undertrained for its size at 300B tokens.

refs.t: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

instructgpt.lead: InstructGPT changed what a large language model is optimised for. In place of next-token likelihood on web text, the final stage maximises a reward model fitted to human comparisons of outputs, and the result was that labelers preferred a 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT model's answers to those of the 175B GPT-3 baseline, a model over a hundred times its size. Every widely deployed assistant since is a variation on its three-stage pipeline.

blocks.h: The objective is not the intent
blocks.b:
Pretraining makes a model a good continuation of internet text. That is a proxy for being useful, and the gap shows in specific ways: asked a question, GPT-3 may continue with a list of further questions, because that is what a list of questions looks like; it will follow a false premise; it will invent citations with the same fluency it uses for true ones.

The paper is precise that this is **an objective mismatch rather than a capability gap** — the model can produce the wanted answer, and nothing in training selects for it. Few-shot prompting was the standing workaround, forcing the format by example, and it is fragile, consumes context, and cannot express what a good answer is.

First, supervised fine-tuning on labeler-written demonstrations, for prompts the labelers largely wrote themselves to bootstrap the first model; real API traffic supplies most of the prompts at the two later stages. Second, a reward model: for each prompt, $K$ sampled completions (between four and nine) are ranked by one labeler, giving $\binom{K}{2}$ pairwise comparisons that are put in a single batch to prevent overfitting. A 6B model with a scalar head is trained under a Bradley–Terry likelihood,

$\mathcal{L} = -\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w,y_l)}\left[\log \sigma\!\left(r_\theta(x,y_w) - r_\theta(x,y_l)\right)\right]$

where $y_w$ is the preferred completion and $r_\theta$ the learned scalar. Third, PPO fine-tunes the policy against $r_\theta$. Ranking is the load-bearing choice: labelers cannot write the best answer to most prompts, but they can reliably say which of two is better.

Maximising a learned reward means maximising an approximation, and a sufficiently good optimiser will find the regions where the approximation is wrong. The objective therefore adds a per-token KL penalty back to the supervised policy and a share of the original pretraining gradient:

$\mathbb{E}\left[r_\theta(x,y) - \beta \log \frac{\pi^{\mathrm{RL}}_\phi(y \mid x)}{\pi^{\mathrm{SFT}}(y \mid x)}\right] + \gamma\, \mathbb{E}_{x \sim D_{\mathrm{pretrain}}}\left[\log \pi^{\mathrm{RL}}_\phi(x)\right]$

$\beta$ holds the policy near the distribution on which the reward model was fitted; $\gamma$ exists because pure preference optimisation degraded academic benchmark scores — the alignment tax. Labelers preferred the aligned models by a wide margin, truthfulness on adversarial questions improved substantially, and toxicity fell when the model was asked to be respectful. Bias benchmarks moved very little.

The reward model is a fixed approximation of a moving policy, and over-optimisation is measurable: past some KL distance, true preference falls while the proxy reward keeps rising. Later work fitted scaling laws to exactly that curve.

The cost is three training runs plus a standing labelling operation, and the alignment is to some forty contractors working from one organisation's written instructions — the paper says so, and does not claim otherwise.

What survived: hallucination, susceptibility to well-framed harmful requests, and learned hedging and verbosity because those are rewarded. DPO later removed the reward model by deriving the optimal policy in closed form and reducing preference learning to a classification loss; Constitutional AI replaced human comparisons with model-generated ones.

refs.t: Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback
Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences

bert.lead: BERT pretrained a deep bidirectional Transformer encoder by deleting tokens from the input and asking the model to reconstruct them, so every layer conditions on left and right context at once. Fine-tuned with a single added output layer, it lifted the GLUE benchmark by around seven points and pushed SQuAD past the reported human score, and for several years "put a head on a pretrained encoder" was simply how NLP was done.

blocks.h: Why left-to-right was not just a habit
blocks.b:
A standard language model must be causal: with full self-attention over the sequence, a token asked to predict itself has already seen itself, and the objective becomes vacuous. That is why GPT-1 masked the future.

ELMo obtained a kind of bidirectionality by training separate left-to-right and right-to-left LSTM language models and concatenating their states, but the two are trained independently and joined only at the top. Neither direction's internal representation is ever computed with knowledge of the other, so the bidirectionality is shallow.

For token-level work — extracting an answer span, tagging an entity — the disambiguating evidence sits on both sides at every layer. **The fix had to be a different objective, not a different architecture.**

Fifteen per cent of WordPiece tokens are selected and predicted from the full surrounding context. Replacing all of them with a `[MASK]` symbol would be simplest, but `[MASK]` never occurs during fine-tuning, so the model would be adapted to an input distribution it never sees again.

The compromise: a selected token becomes `[MASK]` 80% of the time, a random token 10% of the time, and is left unchanged 10% of the time. Because the model cannot tell which case applies at any position, it must maintain a contextual representation of every token rather than only of the corrupted ones, and the random substitutions force some capacity to correct rather than merely copy.

The cost is supervision density: only 15% of positions produce a training signal, so convergence takes more steps than a causal LM needs.

Inference and question answering are relations between two spans, so the input is formatted as `[CLS] A [SEP] B [SEP]` with a learned segment embedding marking each side. A second pretraining objective asks whether B genuinely followed A in the corpus, with a negative sampled half the time, which gives the `[CLS]` position a reason to summarise the pair.

Fine-tuning then updates every parameter for a few epochs with one linear layer on top — the `[CLS]` vector for classification, per-token vectors for span start and end. The same body serves GLUE, SQuAD and named-entity recognition, which is the practical reason the recipe spread so fast. Base and Large were trained on BooksCorpus and English Wikipedia.

Next-sentence prediction turned out to contribute little: RoBERTa dropped it, trained longer on more data with masks resampled each epoch, and improved across the board — evidence BERT was undertrained rather than mis-designed. ALBERT replaced it with sentence-order prediction, a harder discrimination.

XLNet objected that MLM predicts masked positions independently given the context, so structure between two masked tokens is never modelled, and proposed permutation language modelling instead. ELECTRA attacked the sparse supervision by discriminating replaced tokens at every position.

The deeper limit is that an encoder cannot generate: there is no decoding order to sample from. Summarisation and dialogue stayed with decoders, and it was the decoder family that eventually took the general-purpose seat.

refs.t: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach

flashattn.lead: FlashAttention made exact attention several times faster by changing not the arithmetic but the memory traffic. Its observation is that attention on a GPU is bound by reads and writes to high-bandwidth memory rather than by floating-point work, so the fix is to never materialise the $n \times n$ score matrix at all: tile the computation into on-chip SRAM, and recompute what the backward pass needs instead of storing it.

blocks.b:
By 2021 the efficient-attention literature had produced a long list of ways to reduce attention's $O(n^2)$ arithmetic — sparse patterns, low-rank projections, kernel approximations. The FLOP reductions were real; the wall-clock gains often were not, and the approximations cost quality.

The reason is in the memory hierarchy. A standard implementation writes $S = QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d}$ to HBM, reads it back to apply the softmax, writes the result, then reads it again to multiply by $V$. That is $O(n^2)$ traffic in a matrix that is never wanted for its own sake. On an A100, on-chip SRAM is roughly an order of magnitude faster than HBM but holds only tens of megabytes. **The kernel spends most of its time waiting on memory**, so counting FLOPs measures the wrong thing.

The obstacle to tiling is that the softmax normalises across a whole row, which appears to require every score before any output can be written. The online softmax removes that dependency by carrying a running maximum $m$ and running denominator $\ell$ and rescaling the accumulated output when a new block raises the maximum:

$m^{\mathrm{new}} = \max(m, \tilde{m}), \qquad \ell^{\mathrm{new}} = e^{m - m^{\mathrm{new}}}\ell + e^{\tilde{m} - m^{\mathrm{new}}}\tilde{\ell}$

with the partial output scaled by the same factor $e^{m - m^{\mathrm{new}}}$. FlashAttention splits $K$ and $V$ into blocks; for each, it loops over blocks of $Q$, updating each output block and its running softmax statistics in place, and keeps only the output and a per-row log-sum-exp — FlashAttention-2 later swapped the loops so that $Q$ is the outer one and the accumulator never leaves the chip. HBM accesses fall from $O(n^2)$ to roughly $O(n^2 d^2 / M)$ for SRAM of size $M$. The result is exact attention rather than an approximation — the same function as standard attention, computed in a different summation order and so agreeing with it up to floating-point rounding.

The backward pass needs the attention probabilities. Rather than keep them, FlashAttention stores only the output and the $O(n)$ log-sum-exp statistics and rebuilds the scores on chip from $Q$, $K$ and $V$. This performs strictly more arithmetic than a conventional backward pass and is still faster, because the extra FLOPs are close to free against the memory traffic they avoid.

The side effect mattered as much as the speed: activation memory for attention becomes linear rather than quadratic in sequence length. Training runs reported around a threefold speedup on GPT-2 and a clear margin over the then-current MLPerf BERT-large record, and contexts that had been impractical became routine — including the first Transformer to beat chance on Path-X at 16K tokens.

The FLOP count is untouched. FlashAttention is still quadratic in sequence length, and at very long contexts compute reasserts itself as the binding constraint, which is why linear-time architectures continued to be pursued alongside it.

It is also a hand-written kernel welded to one memory hierarchy. FlashAttention-2 rebalanced work across thread blocks and warps and cut non-matmul operations; FlashAttention-3 was rewritten again for Hopper's asynchronous copy engines and FP8. Each generation of accelerator needs the port redone.

The durable contribution is methodological. **IO-awareness became a design criterion rather than an implementation detail**, and the same accounting shows up afterwards in paged KV caches, fused normalisation and activation kernels, and the attention paths now shipped inside every serious framework.

refs.t: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning

s4.lead: S4 took the linear state-space model of classical control, gave it a parameterisation that could actually be trained and evaluated at sequence length, and showed it carrying dependencies across sixteen thousand steps on a task where every attention and recurrent baseline sat at chance. The mechanism that made this practical is a structured decomposition of the state matrix that turns an intractable kernel computation into a Cauchy-kernel evaluation.

blocks.b:
A state-space layer maps a scalar input signal to a scalar output through a hidden state:

$x'(t) = Ax(t) + Bu(t), \qquad y(t) = Cx(t)$

Discretising with a step size gives $x_k = \bar{A}x_{k-1} + \bar{B}u_k$, $y_k = \bar{C}x_k$. This can be run as a recurrence, which costs constant time and memory per step at generation, or unrolled into a convolution with kernel $\bar{K} = (\bar{C}\bar{B}, \bar{C}\bar{A}\bar{B}, \dots, \bar{C}\bar{A}^{L-1}\bar{B})$ and applied to the whole sequence with an FFT during training. **The same parameters serve parallel training and sequential inference**, which is precisely what an RNN cannot offer and a Transformer offers only at quadratic cost. The difficulty is producing $\bar{K}$: computing $L$ powers of $\bar{A}$ naively is both expensive and numerically unstable.

blocks.h: The state matrix is not free
blocks.b:
A randomly initialised or freely learned $A$ produces a layer with no more effective memory than an ordinary RNN — the state decays and old information is gone. The HiPPO framework supplied a specific $A$ derived by asking what matrix makes the state the coefficients of an optimal polynomial projection of the input history under a chosen weighting. Under that matrix the hidden state is a continuously maintained compression of everything the layer has seen, with an explicit approximation guarantee rather than an empirical hope.

The immediate predecessor, the Linear State Space Layer, used HiPPO directly and reproduced the long-memory behaviour, but was far too slow and memory-hungry to be used as a general layer. S4's problem was therefore narrow and concrete: keep HiPPO's memory, make it computable.

HiPPO's matrix is not normal and cannot be stably diagonalised, so the obvious shortcut is unavailable. S4 writes it instead as normal plus low rank, $A = \Lambda - PQ^{*}$, and never forms the kernel entry by entry. It evaluates the kernel's generating function at the roots of unity, where the awkward matrix powers collapse into a single resolvent:

$\hat{K}(z) = \sum_{k} \bar{C}\bar{A}^{k}\bar{B}\, z^{k} = \bar{C}(I - \bar{A}z)^{-1}\bar{B}$

The Woodbury identity reduces the low-rank correction to a shift of the diagonal case, and what remains is a Cauchy matrix–vector product with well-known fast algorithms. An inverse FFT recovers the kernel. Total cost is near-linear in state size plus sequence length, $\tilde{O}(N+L)$, against the $O(N^2L)$ operations and $O(NL)$ space of the naive route — a large enough change to move the method from demonstration to layer.

blocks.h: The linearity it could not escape
blocks.b:
S4 was the first model to rise above chance on Path-X, classified raw speech waveforms without a spectrogram front end, and did well on long sequential image tasks. But $A$, $B$ and $C$ are the same at every position and independent of what the layer is reading, so the whole thing is a fixed convolution. It can remember, but it cannot decide what is worth remembering: **selective copying and induction-style tasks, trivial for attention, are structurally out of reach**, and language modelling quality lagged.

The implementation was also forbidding — complex arithmetic, Cauchy kernels, careful initialisation. Diagonal variants such as DSS and S4D showed most of the quality survives a much simpler parameterisation, S5 moved to a parallel scan, and H3 attacked the language-modelling gap. Mamba resolved the deeper issue by discarding time invariance altogether.

refs.t: Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces
HiPPO: Recurrent Memory with Optimal Polynomial Projections

mamba.lead: Mamba made the state-space model's parameters functions of the input — the one thing S4's mathematics forbade — and paid for it by surrendering the FFT convolution. In its place is a parallel scan written to keep the recurrent state in on-chip memory, and the resulting model matched Transformers of roughly twice its size at the billion-parameter scale while training in linear time and generating with constant memory per step.

blocks.b:
An S4 layer applies the same convolution kernel regardless of content. That is what makes the FFT applicable and what makes the layer useless for anything content-addressed. Two toy tasks isolate it: selective copying, where the tokens to reproduce are marked by their content rather than their position, and induction heads, where a model must notice a bigram and reuse its continuation later. Attention does both by construction; a fixed convolution cannot do either, and induction heads are understood to be a substrate of in-context learning.

On the other side, the Transformer's own costs were unchanged — attention quadratic in sequence length during training, and a KV cache growing linearly with context that dominates memory during deployment. Neither family had both properties.

Mamba makes $\Delta$, $B$ and $C$ linear projections of the current token, leaving $A$ diagonal and shared. Discretisation then varies per position, with $\bar{A}_t = \exp(\Delta_t A)$ and a matching $\bar{B}_t$, so the recurrence $x_t = \bar{A}_t x_{t-1} + \bar{B}_t u_t$ has coefficients that depend on what is being read.

$\Delta_t$ carries most of the work. A large step means the current input dominates and the accumulated state is effectively flushed; a step near zero means the input is ignored and the state persists unchanged. **The familiar gate of an LSTM or GRU falls out of the discretisation rather than being posited**, which is the cleanest argument in the paper: selection is not an addition to the state-space formalism but the consequence of letting its one free timescale vary.

blocks.h: Why the kernel had to be hand-written
blocks.b:
With time-varying coefficients there is no global convolution kernel and no FFT. The recurrence remains associative, so a work-efficient parallel scan applies — but the state is $N$ times wider than the sequence itself, and writing it to HBM would consume the entire benefit. This is FlashAttention's accounting applied to a different operator.

Mamba fuses discretisation, scan and output projection into a single kernel: load the projected inputs into SRAM, run the scan there, write only the output, and recompute intermediate states during the backward pass rather than storing them. The surrounding architecture is deliberately plain — one homogeneous block, a gated MLP wrapped around the selective SSM, with no separate attention or feed-forward alternation.

blocks.h: A fixed state is still a fixed state
blocks.b:
