Mamba reported roughly fivefold generation throughput against a comparable Transformer, competitive language modelling against dense baselines of about twice the parameter count at the scales tested, and strong results on DNA and raw audio where sequences are long and tokenisation is unnatural.

Selection decides what to keep; it does not enlarge what can be kept. Everything must fit a fixed-size summary, so tasks requiring verbatim recall of arbitrary earlier content — multi-query associative recall, dictionary lookup, long-context retrieval — degrade in a way attention does not. The practical answer has been hybrids: interleaving a small number of attention layers, as in Jamba, Samba and Zamba, restores copying at modest cost. Mamba-2's state space duality then recast selective SSMs and a masked form of attention as two readings of the same structured-matrix product, which permitted matmul-heavy kernels and much larger states.

refs.t: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
Transformers are SSMs: Generalized Models and Efficient Algorithms Through Structured State Space Duality

moe.lead: The sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts layer broke the assumption that parameters and compute per example must rise together. A trainable gate sends each token to a handful of expert sub-networks out of thousands, so a layer can hold three orders of magnitude more parameters while the arithmetic each token triggers barely moves. Capacity became something one could buy without buying FLOPs.

blocks.b:
The idea dates to the mixture-of-experts work of the early 1990s and was revisited repeatedly through the 2010s, always with disappointing results. The obstacles were practical rather than conceptual.

Accelerators want large dense matrix products, and data-dependent branching is exactly what breaks them. Gating is a discrete choice, so it is not obvious what gradient the gate should receive. Splitting a batch across $n$ experts leaves each expert a fraction of the examples, and small batches are the regime hardware handles worst. And earlier attempts used a few experts, where the capacity gained is too small to repay any of this trouble. **The contribution was making the idea survive contact with the hardware**, at a scale where the payoff was large enough to notice.

The gate scores every expert, adds trainable per-expert Gaussian noise, keeps the best $k$ and sets the rest to $-\infty$ before the softmax, so their weights are exactly zero and those experts are never evaluated:

$G(x) = \mathrm{softmax}(\mathrm{KeepTopK}(H(x), k)), \qquad y = \sum_{i \in \mathrm{top}k} G(x)_i E_i(x)$

Two choices deserve their reasons. The noise is tunable per expert and smooths the ranking, giving the load-balancing machinery a continuous quantity to act on. And $k$ was taken to be at least two: with $k = 1$ the softmax over a single retained logit is identically one, so the gate appeared to receive no signal about the relative merit of its choice. That reasoning stood for four years before Switch tested it.

Routing is self-reinforcing. An expert favoured early receives more gradient, becomes better, and is favoured more; left alone the distribution collapses onto a few experts while the remainder go untrained. Two auxiliary losses counter it — an importance term penalising the squared coefficient of variation of the summed gate weights per expert across a batch, and a separate load term, since equal total importance can still hide very unequal token counts.

The shrinking-batch problem was solved by a change of parallelism rather than of algorithm. Experts are distributed across devices, and every device ships its tokens to the device owning the chosen expert, so each expert sees tokens pooled from the whole data-parallel batch. That exchange is an all-to-all, which makes the layer's speed a function of the interconnect.

blocks.h: What it proved, and what it left open
blocks.b:
The largest configurations placed MoE layers between stacked LSTMs with over a hundred billion parameters in the experts alone, and reported better perplexity on billion-word-scale corpora at comparable compute, plus translation gains over Google's production NMT system at lower training cost. The claim that capacity and compute could be decoupled was no longer speculative.

The recipe stayed delicate. The balancing losses needed tuning, all-to-all made performance sensitive to cluster topology, training was less stable than a dense model at reduced precision, and expert utilisation had to be watched. GShard carried the layer into the Transformer with explicit capacity factors and sharding annotations; Switch then removed the second expert, addressed the precision instability directly, and pushed the parameter count past a trillion.

refs.t: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
GShard: Scaling Giant Models with Conditional Computation and Automatic Sharding

switch.lead: The Switch Transformer replaced each feed-forward block with a bank of experts and routed every token to exactly one — the configuration the mixture-of-experts literature had assumed could not train. Dropping the second expert cut router arithmetic, halved the buffer each expert must be sized for and halved the all-to-all traffic; with a handful of stability fixes the same recipe reached 1.6 trillion parameters.

blocks.b:
The standing argument against top-1 routing was that the gate would receive no learning signal: a softmax over one retained logit is constant, so nothing tells the router whether its choice was good.

The counter-observation is that the router's probability still multiplies the expert output, $y = p_i(x)\,E_i(x)$, so the loss gradient flows into $p_i$ and raises or lowers the chosen expert's score according to whether it helped. That is a weaker signal than comparing two experts, but it is not zero, and empirically it sufficed. **The savings then compound**: one expert evaluated instead of two, expert capacity buffers halved, and half the tokens crossing the network. At fixed compute those savings buy more experts, which is where the quality comes from.

Because experts live on different devices, each needs a fixed-size buffer allocated before routing is known. Switch sets it as the tokens per batch divided by the number of experts, multiplied by a capacity factor above one. Tokens that overflow their expert's buffer are dropped — passed to the next layer through the residual connection with no expert applied at all. The capacity factor is therefore an explicit dial between wasted padding and lost computation.

Balance is enforced by an auxiliary loss over the $N$ experts,

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aux}} = \alpha N \sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i P_i$

where $f_i$ is the fraction of tokens dispatched to expert $i$ and $P_i$ the mean router probability assigned to it. The product is minimised by a uniform split, and it is differentiable through $P$ even though $f$ is not. A coefficient of about $0.01$ balanced the load without visibly distorting the language-modelling objective.

Sparse models diverged when trained in bfloat16, and the diagnosis was unusually specific. The router exponentiates its logits, and bfloat16's short mantissa means small round-off changes both which expert wins and the gate value that scales its output; that noise compounds through training.

The fix is local: cast to float32 inside the router only, and keep the float32 tensor from ever crossing a device boundary, so no additional communication is incurred. Alongside it, the initialisation scale was reduced, and fine-tuning used much heavier dropout inside the experts than elsewhere — a sparse model carries an enormous parameter count relative to a small downstream dataset, and overfits accordingly.

blocks.h: Results, and the seams that remained
blocks.b:
Against a dense T5 baseline at matched FLOPs per token, Switch reached the same quality in roughly a seventh of the training time; Switch-C, with 2048 experts, ran at 1.6 trillion parameters; gains held across the multilingual mT5 language set. Distillation back into a dense student recovered about a third of the sparse gain at roughly a twentieth of the size, which is the honest measure of how much of the benefit is portable.

What stayed unsolved was memory and routing. Every parameter must be resident even though few are used per token, so serving cost tracks total parameters rather than active ones. Token dropping and capacity tuning persisted. ST-MoE added a router z-loss for stability, expert-choice routing inverted the assignment so that experts select tokens and load balances perfectly by construction — at the cost of some tokens being picked by several experts and others by none — and Mixtral returned to top-2 routing in an openly released model.

refs.t: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
ST-MoE: Designing Stable and Transferable Sparse Expert Models

nnlm.lead: Bengio and colleagues replaced the count table at the heart of language modelling with a neural network that learns a real-valued vector for every word. Because words that behave alike end up near each other in that space, probability mass learned from one sentence transfers to sentences never seen — the generalisation a back-off n-gram can only imitate by redistributing counts.

blocks.b:
A trigram model estimates $P(w_t \mid w_{t-1}, w_{t-2})$ by counting, and everything interesting about it is the smoothing scheme that decides what to do when the count is zero. Back-off and Kneser–Ney discounting move mass to unseen triples by consulting shorter contexts, which is a statement about frequency and nothing else. The model has no space in which cat and dog are close, so having seen "the cat is walking in the bedroom" it knows nothing about "a dog was running in a room".

The failure is combinatorial rather than a shortage of data. With a vocabulary of $100{,}000$ and a ten-word context there are on the order of $10^{50}$ sequences to score, and any corpus leaves essentially all of them at zero.

Each of the $n-1$ preceding words is mapped through a shared matrix $C \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times m}$, with $m$ of order 30 to 100, into a feature vector; the vectors are concatenated into $x$ and the whole vocabulary is scored through one hidden layer,

$y = b + Wx + U\tanh(d + Hx)$

followed by a softmax over $y$. The row $C(w)$ is the same wherever $w$ falls in the window, so a word's representation is estimated from every context it ever appears in rather than once per position. That sharing is where the generalisation comes from: gradient descent has an incentive to move interchangeable words together, and once they are together the probability assigned to one sentence drags its neighbours with it. The $Wx$ term is a direct feature-to-output connection and is not essential.

Every step normalises over the whole vocabulary, so the output layer dominates both the forward pass and the gradient, scaling with $|V|$. The experiments — the Brown corpus of roughly a million words, and a larger set of Associated Press newswire — ran for weeks on a cluster of CPUs, and the paper spends real effort on splitting the output layer across machines.

That cost set the agenda for the following decade. Hierarchical softmax replaced flat normalisation with a tree of binary decisions; importance sampling estimated the denominator's gradient from a few sampled words instead, and noise-contrastive estimation and finally negative sampling dropped normalisation altogether in favour of discrimination against those samples. The perplexity gain over a well-smoothed trigram was real but not dramatic, and the best numbers came from interpolating the two models, which failed on different sentences.

The fixed context was inherited rather than questioned. The Markov assumption of the n-gram survives intact — only the estimator changed — so nothing before the $n-1$ given words can be conditioned on, and long-range agreement or topic stays out of reach. Recurrent language models removed the window a few years later by carrying state instead of a context buffer.

The other legacy was accidental. $C$ was a nuisance parameter here, a means to a probability. The field then decided it was the product. word2vec kept the table, threw away the hidden layer and the exact normalisation, and trained on corpora orders of magnitude larger — the same architecture with the expensive parts deleted.

refs.t: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model

w2v.lead: word2vec is what remains of a neural language model once everything expensive is removed: no hidden layer, no normalisation over the vocabulary, and an objective that is binary classification against a handful of random words. It trained on billions of tokens on a single machine, and the vectors turned out to support linear analogy arithmetic that nobody had designed in.

blocks.b:
Two models were proposed. CBOW averages the vectors of the surrounding words and predicts the centre; skip-gram does the reverse, predicting each context word from the centre, and maximises

$\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{-c \le j \le c,\, j \ne 0} \log p(w_{t+j} \mid w_t)$

The window size is resampled uniformly from $1$ to $c$ for each token, which weights nearer words more heavily without a separate weighting term. There is no nonlinearity anywhere: the model is two lookup tables and a dot product. Bengio's network spent most of its compute in the tanh layer and the full softmax, and the wager here was that neither was buying anything the embedding table needed. Removing them turned a cluster job into a laptop job.

The remaining cost was the softmax denominator, and skip-gram with negative sampling replaces it outright. For an observed pair the objective is

$\log \sigma(v'^{\top}_{w_O} v_{w_I}) + \sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbb{E}_{w_i \sim P_n(w)}\left[\log \sigma(-v'^{\top}_{w_i} v_{w_I})\right]$

— push the true context word up, push $k$ sampled words down. Nothing is normalised, so the per-step cost is $k+1$ dot products rather than $|V|$; $k$ around 5 to 20 suits a small corpus, 2 to 5 a large one. The noise distribution is the unigram raised to the power $3/4$, which outperformed both the plain unigram and the uniform in the authors' experiments and was never given a principled justification. Frequent tokens are also discarded with probability $1-\sqrt{t/f(w)}$, which both saves time and effectively widens the window past the function words.

blocks.h: Analogies, and what they turned out to be
blocks.b:
The vectors placed $\mathrm{vec}(\text{king}) - \mathrm{vec}(\text{man}) + \mathrm{vec}(\text{woman})$ nearest to queen, and did so across thousands of semantic and syntactic analogy questions. This was an observation, not an objective: nothing in the loss asks for parallel offsets.

Later analysis tempered both the mystery and the framing. Levy and Goldberg showed that skip-gram with negative sampling is implicitly factorising a word–context matrix of pointwise mutual information shifted by $\log k$, which makes the fashionable opposition between predictive and count-based embeddings largely a difference of loss function and weighting. The analogy result itself is partly an artefact of the evaluation, which excludes the three query words from the answer set.

A word type gets exactly one point, so every sense of bank is averaged into it in proportion to corpus frequency, and the downstream model must undo that from scratch. Morphology is invisible — runs, running and runner are unrelated strings — and anything outside the training vocabulary has no vector at all. fastText attacked both by summing character n-grams; ELMo and then BERT attacked the first properly by making the vector a function of the sentence.

The vectors also absorbed whatever regularities the corpus contained, including occupational gender stereotypes recoverable by the same analogy arithmetic that made them famous, which opened a line of work on measuring and removing such structure.

refs.t: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space
Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality

glove.lead: GloVe fits word vectors to corpus-wide co-occurrence counts instead of to a stream of local prediction problems. Its premise is that meaning is carried by ratios of co-occurrence probabilities rather than by the probabilities themselves, and the model is the weighted least-squares problem you get when you require a dot product to reproduce the logarithm of a count.

blocks.b:
Take ice and steam and probe them with other words. Both co-occur often with water and rarely with fashion, so raw probabilities separate nothing. The ratio $P(k \mid \text{ice})/P(k \mid \text{steam})$ is large for solid, small for gas, and near $1$ for both water and fashion — it distinguishes the words that discriminate the pair from those that do not.

Demanding that a vector space encode that ratio, and that it do so linearly in the difference of the two word vectors, forces the form of the model. Exponentiating the linear relation and absorbing the row and column normalisers into biases gives $w_i^{\top}\tilde w_k + b_i + \tilde b_k = \log X_{ik}$, where $X_{ik}$ is the number of times $k$ occurs in the context of $i$.

That equation is imposed as a regression over the co-occurrence matrix,

$J = \sum_{i,j=1}^{V} f(X_{ij})\left(w_i^{\top}\tilde w_j + b_i + \tilde b_j - \log X_{ij}\right)^2$

with $f(x) = (x/x_{\max})^{\alpha}$ below a cutoff and $1$ above, using $x_{\max}=100$ and $\alpha = 3/4$. The weighting does two jobs. Since $f(0)=0$, zero counts contribute nothing and the sum can run only over observed pairs, a small fraction of $V^2$; and the cap stops a handful of extremely frequent pairs from dominating the loss. This is the difference from the earlier matrix methods: latent semantic analysis applies SVD, which weights every cell equally, including the enormous number of uninformative near-zero ones. Counting is done once up front, so training then scales with the number of non-zero entries rather than with corpus length.

GloVe reported better analogy and word-similarity scores than skip-gram at matched dimension and corpus, and the framing — global counts beating local prediction — was widely repeated. Levy, Goldberg and Dagan then showed that most of the reported differences across this whole family came from hyperparameters and preprocessing that had migrated unevenly between implementations: dynamic context windows, subsampling of frequent words, the shift applied to PMI, and the habit of summing the word and context vectors, $w + \tilde w$, which GloVe used and the others generally did not. Held constant, GloVe's reported edge disappeared — skip-gram with negative sampling came out ahead of it on every task they tested — and across the family as a whole no approach held a global advantage. The durable contribution is the demonstration that predictive and count-based embeddings are fitting the same co-occurrence statistics under different losses.

Everything word2vec left unsolved, GloVe leaves unsolved as well. There is still one vector per string, so polysemy is averaged away and out-of-vocabulary words have nothing; morphology is still invisible; and the co-occurrence matrix must be rebuilt from scratch to add data, with memory proportional to the observed pairs — for web-scale corpora, the largest object in the pipeline.

What it did do is supply the era's default input layer. Pretrained 300-dimensional GloVe vectors on Wikipedia and Common Crawl were the standard initialisation for the LSTM models of 2015 to 2017, and they were displaced only when the embedding stopped being a fixed table and became a function of the surrounding sentence.

refs.t: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation

fasttext.lead: fastText represents a word as the sum of the vectors of its character n-grams, so morphology is built into the embedding table rather than left for each inflected form to learn independently. A word never seen in training still has a vector, because its pieces have been seen thousands of times.

blocks.b:
Skip-gram and GloVe estimate a distinct vector per string from that string's occurrences alone. Word frequencies are Zipfian, so most of the vocabulary appears a handful of times and most vectors are correspondingly poor, while anything outside the vocabulary gets nothing at all and the downstream system falls back to an unknown-word token.

In English this is a nuisance. In Finnish, Turkish, Czech or German it is disabling, because inflection and compounding multiply the number of types while keeping each one rare — the same lemma is split across dozens of strings, each individually undertrained. To skip-gram, run, runs, running and runner are four unrelated symbols, and the shared stem is information sitting in plain view that the model discards.

Each word is bracketed with boundary symbols and decomposed into all character n-grams for $3 \le n \le 6$, plus the full word as its own token: where becomes <wh, whe, her, ere, re>, and <where>. The brackets matter — they keep the n-gram her, taken from where, distinct from the standalone word <her>. The scoring function of skip-gram with negative sampling is then replaced by

$s(w,c) = \sum_{g \in \mathcal{G}_w} z_g^{\top} v_c$

where $\mathcal{G}_w$ is the word's n-gram set and $z_g$ its vector; the rest of the training procedure is untouched. The n-gram inventory is far larger than the word vocabulary, so n-grams are hashed into a fixed number of buckets — two million in the released models — trading collisions for bounded memory.

blocks.h: Where it helps and where it hurts
blocks.b:
The gains concentrate exactly where the argument predicts: morphologically rich languages, rare words, and syntactic analogies, where the n-grams effectively encode the suffix being tested. On English semantic analogies the improvement is small and sometimes negative, because character overlap is a noisy proxy for meaning and will happily pull together words that share substrings and nothing else.

Because the representation is compositional at the character level, misspellings, inflections and unseen compounds all receive sensible vectors, which is why fastText became the practical default for noisy web text and for languages without a large clean corpus. Its classification sibling — a linear model over bag-of-n-gram features with a hierarchical softmax — matched small neural text classifiers while training on a CPU in seconds.

Character n-grams are morphology only in the crudest sense. They carry no notion of a morpheme boundary, cannot represent suppletion such as go and went, and cannot separate a genuine affix from a coincidence of spelling. And the deeper problem is untouched: the vector for bank is still a single point, fixed before the sentence is read.

What survived is not the embedding table but the decomposition. Subword units moved into the tokeniser — byte-pair encoding, WordPiece, SentencePiece — where the model itself composes the pieces through its own layers rather than by summing a lookup. That removes out-of-vocabulary words from the vocabulary altogether instead of patching over them at the embedding.

refs.t: Enriching Word Vectors with Subword Information
Bag of Tricks for Efficient Text Classification

elmo.lead: ELMo made a word's vector a function of the sentence containing it. A two-layer bidirectional LSTM language model is pretrained on unlabelled text, and each downstream task learns its own weighted average of that model's internal states — a representation of a token in context, rather than a lookup by string.

blocks.b:
Every static embedding assigns one vector per string, so play in a theatre and play in a match share a single point that is a frequency-weighted compromise between the senses. Task models papered over this with their own recurrent encoders trained on labelled data, which are minuscule beside the unlabelled text available.

CoVe had already shown that the hidden states of a pretrained encoder could be used as contextual features, but it drew its supervision from machine translation and was therefore capped by the size of available parallel corpora. A language model needs nothing but raw text. That is the argument ELMo makes: the supply of supervision for contextual representation is effectively unlimited, provided the pretraining objective asks only for the next word.

blocks.h: The biLM and the layer mixture
blocks.b:
A forward language model predicts $w_{k+1}$ from the left context and a backward one predicts $w_{k-1}$ from the right; they share the token representation and the softmax and are trained to maximise the sum of the two log-likelihoods. The input layer is a character convolution, so any string — including one never seen — receives a representation.

For $L$ layers there are $2L+1$ vectors per token: the context-independent input plus both directions at each layer. These are collapsed per task as

$\mathrm{ELMo}_k^{\mathrm{task}} = \gamma^{\mathrm{task}}\sum_{j=0}^{L} s_j^{\mathrm{task}}\, \mathbf{h}_{k,j}$

with $s$ softmax-normalised weights over layers and $\gamma$ a scalar for overall scale. Both are learned by the downstream task while the language model stays frozen.

blocks.h: Why the mixture, not the top layer
blocks.b:
The layers are not redundant, and this is the paper's most useful empirical finding. **The lower LSTM layer is the better predictor of part of speech, and the higher layer the better predictor of word sense.** A task dominated by syntax and one dominated by semantics therefore want different mixtures, and earlier work that took the top layer alone — the natural thing to do with a pretrained encoder — was discarding the syntactic layer for free.

In use, ELMo vectors were concatenated to the inputs, and often the outputs, of an existing task architecture with no other change. That was enough to advance the state of the art on question answering, textual entailment, semantic role labelling, coreference, named-entity recognition and sentiment, with substantial relative error reductions across all six.

The two directions are separate models joined only by concatenation at the end. No layer ever computes a state conditioned jointly on left and right context, so a token whose reading depends on evidence from both sides is left for the task model to resolve. ELMo is also a feature extractor rather than a starting point: the language model is frozen, the task model is trained from scratch, and none of the pretrained capacity is available for the task itself.

GPT answered the second objection by fine-tuning the entire stack, and BERT answered both, replacing the directional prediction objective with masked-token prediction so that one deep Transformer conditions on all surrounding context at once. Within roughly a year the LSTM underneath ELMo had gone as well.

refs.t: Deep contextualized word representations

elman.lead: Elman's recurrent network gave a feed-forward net a memory of its own internal state: the hidden layer's activations are copied at each step into a set of context units and fed back as extra input on the next. Time stopped being a spatial window over the input and became something the network carried in its state, which made variable-length sequences representable at all — and made the vanishing-gradient problem the central obstacle in sequence modelling for the next twenty-five years.

blocks.b:
The standard way to give a network temporal context in the late 1980s was to lay time out in space: a sliding window over the input, as in NETtalk, or a tapped delay line, as in the time-delay networks used for phonemes. Three things are wrong with that. The window width fixes in advance the longest dependency the model can represent. The same pattern arriving at two different offsets is a different input vector, so nothing learned at one offset transfers to another. And a sequence longer than the window simply has no encoding.

Jordan's earlier recurrent network fed the network's own output back as context, which limits its memory to what it has already committed to saying. Elman's change was to feed back the hidden layer instead, so the memory could be an internal representation the network was free to shape for itself.

blocks.h: The context layer, and how it was trained
blocks.b:
At each step the hidden activations are copied verbatim into context units — the recurrent connections have weight fixed at $1.0$ and are not learned — and on the following step those units are simply additional inputs alongside $x_t$:

$h_t = \sigma(W_x x_t + W_c h_{t-1} + b), \qquad y_t = g(W_y h_t + c)$

Only $W_x$, $W_c$ and $W_y$ are trained. Crucially, training used ordinary backpropagation with $h_{t-1}$ treated as a fixed input: no gradient was passed through the copy. The network is therefore trained with a one-step truncation of backpropagation through time, and any longer dependency it acquires is acquired indirectly, because the hidden state that shortens today's error also happens to be useful tomorrow. The task throughout is next-item prediction, which needs no labels.

The experiments matter as much as the architecture. Given a stream of consonants where each expands deterministically to a vowel sequence, the network's prediction error spikes at each consonant, which is genuinely unpredictable, then collapses across the vowels — the error curve itself segments the stream. Given sentences generated from templates over a small lexicon, with next-word prediction as the only objective, hierarchical clustering of the hidden-state vectors recovered a nesting nobody had encoded: verbs apart from nouns, animate from inanimate, transitive verbs from intransitive.

The representations were also token-level rather than type-level — the same word occupied different points in hidden space in different sentences. That is the property the whole distributional-representation line later depended on, and it fell out of a prediction objective on unlabelled text.

blocks.h: The gradient it could not carry
blocks.b:
Even trained with full backpropagation through time, the sensitivity of $h_t$ to $h_{t-k}$ is a product of $k$ Jacobians of the form $W_c^{\top}\mathrm{diag}(\sigma')$. With saturating sigmoids $\sigma' \leq 1/4$, so unless the recurrent weights are large the product shrinks geometrically; make them large enough to avoid that and the same product explodes instead. Bengio, Simard and Frasconi made the trade formal in 1994: storing a bit robustly against noise over many steps requires the recurrence to be contracting in the relevant directions, and contraction is exactly what kills the gradient.

In practice Elman networks learned dependencies of about ten steps, and rarely more. Clipping later tamed the explosion; the decay needed an architectural answer, and that was the LSTM's constant error carousel.

refs.t: Finding Structure in Time
Learning Long-Term Dependencies with Gradient Descent is Difficult

lstm.lead: The LSTM replaced the multiplicative recurrence of a plain RNN with an additive one: a memory cell whose self-connection has weight exactly one, so error flowing back through it is neither amplified nor attenuated. Multiplicative gates sit around that cell to decide when it is written to and when it is read from. It is worth saying plainly that the 1997 paper has only input and output gates — the forget gate arrived three years later, from Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins, and it is arguably the single most important component of the unit as used today.

blocks.b:
Hochreiter's 1991 analysis showed that error signal in a recurrent net is scaled at each step by roughly $w\,\sigma'$; below one it decays exponentially, above one it explodes, and there is no setting that holds. But Hochreiter and Schmidhuber identified two further obstacles that a merely linear recurrence would not fix.

The **input weight conflict**: a single incoming weight must both admit inputs that are worth storing and reject the many that are not, and gradient descent pulls it in both directions at once. The symmetric **output weight conflict**: an outgoing weight must both protect the stored value from disturbing downstream units and release it at the one moment it is needed. Both are conflicts about timing, and neither can be resolved by a weight. They need a signal that varies with context — which is what a gate is.

At the centre of the unit is a linear unit with a fixed self-recurrent connection of weight $1.0$. Its local derivative is exactly one, so error injected at step $t$ arrives at step $t-k$ undiminished, whatever $k$ is. Around it, an input gate and an output gate, each a sigmoid unit reading the current input and the previous hidden state, multiply the write path and the read path:

$c_t = c_{t-1} + i_t \odot g(W_c x_t + U_c h_{t-1}), \qquad h_t = o_t \odot \mathrm{tanh}(c_t)$

The gates resolve both conflicts directly: the cell can be sealed against irrelevant input without losing what it holds, and can withhold its contents until the moment they matter. The original learning rule truncated the gradient at the gate inputs, deliberately, to keep the update local in time and constant in cost per step.

A pure carousel has no way to discard. On a continuous stream with no reset, the cell state drifts without bound and the output squash saturates. Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins added a third gate, so the recurrence becomes

$c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{c}_t$

and the per-step multiplier on the gradient is $f_t$ rather than $1$. The network now chooses its own time constant for each cell and can clear one when a segment ends. The modern LSTM is the 1997 unit plus that addition, plus untruncated backpropagation through time and, in some variants, peephole connections. Greff and colleagues' large ablation later found the forget gate and the output nonlinearity to be the two components whose removal consistently hurts; initialising the forget-gate bias positive, so cells default to remembering, is standard for the same reason.

blocks.h: What it unlocked, and the wall it hit
blocks.b:
With CTC it made unconstrained handwriting and large-vocabulary speech recognition work end to end; with the encoder-decoder framing it became the basis of neural machine translation and of production systems by 2016. It remained the default sequence model for close to a decade.

What it never addressed is that the recurrence is serial. Step $t$ cannot begin until $t-1$ finishes, so training does not parallelise over length, and each step is a thin matrix-vector product that leaves a GPU bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound. Attention attacked the fixed-width state; the Transformer attacked the seriality by removing recurrence entirely. The additive carry survived both — as the residual connection, and later as the input-dependent decay of gated linear recurrences that can be evaluated by a parallel scan.

refs.t: Long Short-Term Memory
LSTM: A Search Space Odyssey

gru.lead: The GRU is an LSTM with parts deliberately removed: no separate memory cell, no output gate, and the decisions to write and to erase tied to a single gate so that they sum to one. Cho and colleagues introduced it as a component of their encoder-decoder translation model rather than as a paper in its own right. A decade of comparisons has not established a consistent quality gap in either direction, which is itself the most informative result about what gating was doing.

blocks.h: What was actually wrong with the LSTM
blocks.b:
Nothing about its accuracy. The complaints were cost and opacity. An LSTM layer carries four weight matrices per input and four per recurrent connection, splits its state across a cell vector and a hidden vector, and runs three sigmoid gates whose individual contributions had never been isolated — the 1997 unit and the 2000 forget gate had simply accumulated. In 2014 the models being trained were translation systems where per-step cost multiplies by sequence length and again by corpus size, so a quarter fewer parameters and two fewer nonlinearities per step is a real saving.

Underneath sat a scientific question: of the carousel, the three gates and the two-part state, which parts earn their keep? The GRU is one answer to that question, offered by construction rather than by ablation.

blocks.h: Two gates and a convex combination
blocks.b:
A reset gate $r_t$ controls how much of the previous state enters the candidate; an update gate $z_t$ interpolates between keeping the old state and taking the new one:

$\tilde{h}_t = \mathrm{tanh}(W x_t + U (r_t \odot h_{t-1})), \qquad h_t = z_t \odot h_{t-1} + (1 - z_t) \odot \tilde{h}_t$

The sign convention on $z$ differs between the original paper and most library implementations; the structure does not. Two consequences follow. Input and forget are now tied: the unit cannot write without erasing in equal measure, where an LSTM can add to a cell it is also preserving. And the state is fully exposed — with no output gate there is no way to hold a value while hiding it from the rest of the network. The additive path survives: when $z_t$ approaches one the unit copies its state, and $\partial h_t / \partial h_{t-1} \approx z_t$, a carousel with a learned leak.

Chung and colleagues ran the direct comparison on polyphonic music and raw speech and found GRU and LSTM comparable, with the winner dataset-dependent and both far ahead of a tanh recurrence. Jozefowicz and colleagues then searched over thousands of mutated gated architectures and found none that consistently beat both — and reported that setting the LSTM's forget-gate bias to one removed most of the GRU's apparent advantage on their tasks.

The honest reading is that the specific arrangement of gates matters much less than the presence of a multiplicative gate biased, at initialisation, toward copying the state. The GRU became the default where parameters or step latency were tight, the LSTM where a protected internal value helped, and practitioners stopped treating the choice as consequential.

There is one clean separation. An LSTM's cell is an unbounded accumulator, so at finite precision it can implement a counter; Weiss, Goldberg and Yahav showed that an LSTM trained on $a^n b^n$ generalises to lengths well beyond training, while a GRU, whose state is a convex combination of values bounded by $\mathrm{tanh}$, saturates instead and can only memorise the lengths it has seen. The output gate turns out to matter for the same reason: it lets the cell grow without the growth spilling into the hidden state.

Both units left the larger limitation untouched — computation still walks the sequence one step at a time. By 2017 that was the seam everyone attacked, and the LSTM-versus-GRU question stopped being interesting. The input-dependent decay of a selective state-space model is closer in spirit to the GRU's single interpolation than to the LSTM's separate cell.

refs.t: Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder-Decoder for Statistical Machine Translation
Empirical Evaluation of Gated Recurrent Neural Networks on Sequence Modeling

seq2seq.lead: Sutskever, Vinyals and Le showed that a general sequence transducer could be two LSTMs and nothing else: one reads the source into a single fixed-width vector, the other generates the target conditioned on it. Trained end to end on WMT'14 English-French, an ensemble of five such models reached 34.81 BLEU against 33.30 for a mature phrase-based system — a single model managed 30.59 — with no alignment model, no phrase table and no language-specific engineering anywhere in the pipeline.

blocks.b:
Statistical machine translation was an assembly of separately estimated parts: word and phrase alignment models fitted by expectation-maximisation, a phrase table extracted from those alignments, an n-gram language model trained on monolingual text, a reordering model, and a log-linear combination whose weights were tuned on a development set. Each piece optimised its own objective and none optimised translation quality directly. Neural networks had entered only as rescoring components bolted onto that stack.

The structural obstacle to replacing it wholesale was dimensional. A feed-forward network maps a fixed-size input to a fixed-size output, and translation maps variable to variable with no length correspondence and substantial reordering. Recurrent networks handled labelling problems where output length equals input length; translation is not one of those.

The encoder LSTM consumes the source token by token and is then discarded except for its final state, which serves as a summary vector $v$. A second LSTM with entirely separate parameters is initialised from $v$ and factorises the target autoregressively,

$p(y_1,\dots,y_{T'} \mid x) = \prod_{t=1}^{T'} p(y_t \mid v, y_{<t})$

emitting an end-of-sequence symbol to decide its own length. Training maximises the log-likelihood of reference translations; decoding is a left-to-right beam search, and a beam of two already recovered most of the gain over greedy search. The model was four layers deep with 1000 cells and 1000-dimensional embeddings, a 160k source and 80k target vocabulary, with everything outside those vocabularies mapped to a single unknown token that cost BLEU directly. It trained for about ten days across eight GPUs.

blocks.h: Reversing the source, and what that admitted
blocks.b:
The paper's one trick was to reverse the word order of every source sentence while leaving the target alone. This lifted BLEU by several points and cut test perplexity substantially, and the explanation is precise: reversing leaves the average distance between corresponding source and target words unchanged, but collapses the **minimal lag** — the first few source words now sit adjacent to the first few target words, so the model gets an early foothold and the rest of the sentence follows from it.

That a purely presentational change was worth several BLEU is a statement about how far gradient signal could actually reach through the recurrence, not about the summary vector's capacity. It was the clearest available evidence that distance in the recurrence, and not representational width, was the binding constraint.

Everything about a source sentence must fit into one vector, written once and never revisited; the decoder has no way to look back at the input while generating. Cho and colleagues' companion analysis of the same encoder-decoder family showed BLEU peaking around ten source words and decaying steadily thereafter — well inside the lengths they trained on, and unchanged when they retrained on sentences of up to fifty words — exactly as that account predicts.

Two responses were available: make the summary bigger and better structured, or let the decoder re-read the encoder's states. Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio had already taken the second — their attention paper reached arXiv nine days before this one, answering the same bottleneck in the encoder-decoder line — and the fixed vector disappeared from serious systems almost immediately. What survived untouched is the skeleton — encode, condition, generate one token at a time under a likelihood objective — which is still the shape of the Transformer and of every decoder-only language model since.

refs.t: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
On the Properties of Neural Machine Translation: Encoder-Decoder Approaches

bahdanau.lead: Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio deleted the single summary vector. Their decoder keeps the encoder's entire sequence of states and, at every output step, computes a fresh weighted average over them, with the weights produced by a small network trained jointly with the rest of the model. Alignment stopped being a separate model estimated beforehand and became a differentiable part of translation itself — the mechanism that, once detached from the recurrence around it, became the Transformer.

blocks.b:
The encoder-decoder model of a few months earlier compressed a source sentence of any length into one vector of fixed width. The authors' diagnosis was that the burden on that vector grows with sentence length while its capacity does not, and they demonstrated it directly: their reimplemented baseline held its BLEU on short sentences and degraded steadily on long ones.

The contrast with what the neural model had replaced is sharp. Phrase-based systems had explicit alignment — latent correspondence variables between source and target positions, estimated by expectation-maximisation before translation training began. The neural encoder-decoder had none at all; whatever correspondence existed had to be reconstructed inside a recurrent state that was also carrying everything else. Giving it back, but learned end to end, is the whole of the contribution.

The encoder is a bidirectional RNN, so each source position $j$ yields an annotation $h_j$ concatenating a forward and a backward state and summarising the sentence with a bias toward the word at $j$. At target step $i$ the decoder scores every annotation against its previous state $s_{i-1}$, normalises, and takes the corresponding average:

$e_{ij} = v_a^{\top} \mathrm{tanh}(W_a s_{i-1} + U_a h_j), \qquad \alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp(e_{ij})}{\sum_k \exp(e_{ik})}, \qquad c_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} h_j$

The score is a one-hidden-layer network — additive attention — evaluated once per (target step, source position) pair. Softness is what makes this trainable: because $c_i$ is a smooth function of every annotation, the translation loss supplies gradient to the alignment weights without any alignment supervision. A hard selection would have required a score-function estimator or an EM procedure, and neither was necessary.

The attention model's quality no longer fell away with sentence length, where the fixed-vector baseline's did; on sentences composed entirely of in-vocabulary words it reached parity with the conventional phrase-based system, which no purely neural translator had managed. Perhaps as important, the $\alpha$ matrices could be plotted and inspected: they were broadly monotonic, with clean off-diagonal blocks exactly where the two languages order constituents differently, such as English adjective-noun sequences mapping to French noun-adjective.

That readability drove adoption as much as the BLEU did. It should be held loosely, though — later work has argued at length that attention weights are not a faithful account of what a model's prediction depends on, and treating a bright cell as an explanation is a step the evidence does not support.

The attention itself costs a score evaluation for every source-target position pair, which is quadratic, but it was not the binding cost: the encoder is serial in source length and the decoder serial in target length, so nothing parallelises across time and the RNN dominates. Luong and colleagues shortly replaced the scoring MLP with a dot product or a bilinear form and experimented with restricting attention to a local window, finding comparable quality more cheaply — which established that the alignment mechanism needed very little capacity of its own.

The remaining step was to notice that if attention could give the decoder direct access to any source position, the recurrence was no longer earning its place, and that the encoder could attend to itself in the same way. Less than three years later, the Transformer took it.

refs.t: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation

mixtral.lead: Mixtral 8x7B put a sparse mixture-of-experts model into the open under an Apache 2.0 licence. Every feed-forward block is replaced by eight of them and a router fires two per token, so the network holds roughly 47B parameters while spending the arithmetic of about 13B on any given token. At that cost it matched or beat Llama 2 70B across most benchmarks.

blocks.b:
Sparse routing was not new. GShard and Switch Transformer had established the central trade — send each token to a small subset of a large parameter bank and the parameter count grows without the per-token FLOPs following — and Switch had pushed it past a trillion parameters with top-1 routing.

Those were encoder-decoder models trained inside Google on infrastructure nobody else had, and although Switch's checkpoints were eventually published, nothing openly available was a sparse model you could actually chat with. Everything openly available was dense, which meant paying full compute for every parameter at every token. What remained untested in public was whether the trade still paid at a size a small team could actually serve, in a decoder-only chat model rather than on a masked-language benchmark.

Mixtral keeps the Mistral 7B backbone — grouped-query attention, RMSNorm, rotary embeddings — and swaps each feed-forward block for eight; the sliding-window attention is dropped, and the model attends over a full 32k context. A linear gate $W_g$ maps the token's hidden state to eight logits; the two largest are kept, a softmax is taken over just those two, and the layer output is their weighted sum:

$y = \sum_{i} \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\mathrm{top}2(x W_g)\right)_i \, E_i(x)$

where $E_i$ is the $i$-th SwiGLU expert. The decision is made per token and per layer, so any sequence of length exercises all eight many times over: what is saved is arithmetic, not storage. All 47B parameters must be resident to produce one token. Keeping two rather than one gives the gate a comparison to learn from; Switch showed top-1 can be made to work, but needed care over precision and initialisation to get there.

The name invites a reading the model does not support. The authors looked for topic-level specialisation in the routing over The Pile — an expert that claims mathematics, or code, or biology — and found essentially none; the distribution over experts is close to uniform across domains.

What the routing does show is structure at the level of syntax and position. **Consecutive tokens go to the same expert far more often than chance**, and the effect deepens with the network: repetition at the first layer is close to random, while the middle and final layers sit well above it. The partition the gate learns suits optimisation rather than carving the data at any joint a person would name. That matters practically: you cannot prune away the experts a particular deployment does not need, because there is no such subset.

The saving is in FLOPs alone, and for a served model the binding constraint is usually memory. Mixtral wants the VRAM of a 47B dense model while delivering the quality of something larger and the latency of something much smaller — a good trade on a multi-GPU server, an awkward one on a single card, and the reason expert offloading and expert-parallel serving grew into their own literature.

Training is also less forgiving. A load-balancing auxiliary loss is needed to stop the gate collapsing onto a few experts, and fine-tuning overfits more readily than a dense model of the same active size. Meta chose dense for Llama 3 and cited stability; DeepSeek went the other way, toward many finer-grained experts alongside shared always-on ones.

refs.t: Mixtral of Experts
Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity

llama.lead: LLaMA is a family of dense decoder-only models from 7B to 65B, trained only on publicly available corpora and released with weights. Its argument was economic rather than architectural: Chinchilla's scaling law optimises training compute, but a model that will be served answers vastly more tokens than it was trained on, so the right move is to train a small model long past the point where the loss curve stops paying for itself.

blocks.h: The scaling law it argued with
blocks.b:
Chinchilla had shown that for a fixed training budget, parameters and tokens should scale together, and the field read this as licence to grow both. LLaMA takes the same result and points out what its objective leaves out: **inference cost is absent from the compute-optimal calculation**, and for a deployed model it dominates.

So the 7B and 13B were trained on a trillion tokens and were still improving; the 33B and 65B saw around 1.4T. The outcome was the point. The 13B model outperformed GPT-3 at 175B on most benchmarks, and the 65B was competitive with Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B while being small enough to run on hardware an academic group could obtain.

Nothing in the model is novel and each choice has a stated source. Pre-normalisation with RMSNorm, which drops the mean-centring of LayerNorm and is cheaper for no measured loss. SwiGLU in place of ReLU, from PaLM. Rotary position embeddings rather than learned absolute ones, from GPTNeo.

The engineering carried as much weight as the architecture: a memory-efficient causal attention that never materialises the masked half of the score matrix, and hand-chosen activation checkpointing so the expensive intermediates are stored rather than recomputed. The 65B was trained on 2048 A100s over roughly three weeks. Publishing that recipe, with token counts and throughput, is what let others repeat it.

blocks.h: Public data, and what it settled
blocks.b:
The corpus was CommonCrawl and C4, GitHub, Wikipedia, books, ArXiv and StackExchange, with mixing proportions and filtering published. No licensed or proprietary source was required.

That disposed of the standard defence for closed weights — that the data could not be shared. It did not dispose of the copyright question: the book portion drew on Books3, which later sat at the centre of litigation over the training corpora of several models. "Publicly available" and "cleared for use" turned out to be different claims, and the paper does not distinguish them.

Weights went out under a non-commercial research licence, by application. Within a week they were circulating freely, and the consequences were immediate and almost entirely outside Meta's control: `llama.cpp` and 4-bit quantisation put a usable model on a laptop, LoRA and then QLoRA made fine-tuning a single-GPU exercise, and Alpaca and Vicuna showed what cheap instruction tuning could do on top.

What shipped was a base model only. No instruction tuning beyond a brief ablation, no preference optimisation, no safety work, no commercial licence. LLaMA supplied a substrate and left alignment entirely to whoever downloaded it — which is exactly what made it useful, and exactly what Llama 2 was written to answer.

refs.t: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models

alpaca.lead: Alpaca and Vicuna demonstrated that the visible behaviour of a chat assistant could be transplanted onto an open base model for a few hundred dollars. Alpaca fine-tuned LLaMA 7B on 52,000 instruction–response pairs generated by an OpenAI model; blind comparison put it roughly level with the teacher on the evaluation set used. The year that followed was spent working out what that comparison did and did not measure.

blocks.b:
InstructGPT's recipe needed a paid annotation workforce writing demonstrations, a second round of humans ranking model outputs, a reward model fitted to those rankings, and a PPO loop. Every stage was expensive and the whole thing was out of reach for a university group.

Self-Instruct had already shown a model could bootstrap instruction data from a small seed set. Alpaca's contribution was to point that pipeline at a much stronger teacher: 175 hand-written seed tasks, `text-davinci-003` asked to generate new instructions and their responses, light filtering for duplicates, 52K pairs, then ordinary supervised fine-tuning. **No reward model, no reinforcement learning, and three hours of training.**

LMSYS took LLaMA 13B and fine-tuned it on roughly 70,000 conversations users had voluntarily shared from ChatGPT. Two differences from Alpaca mattered: the data were multi-turn, and they came from the real distribution of what people ask rather than from a synthesiser's idea of it.

The evaluation proved more consequential than the model. Lacking any benchmark for open-ended chat, they had GPT-4 compare pairs of responses and score them, reporting Vicuna at around ninety per cent of ChatGPT's quality. LLM-as-judge was cheap and agreed with human raters often enough to be adopted everywhere, and it grew into MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena. Its biases — toward the first-presented answer, and toward length — were documented later by the same group.

The follow-up work was unkind. Scaling imitation data was found to leave human preference scores flat once they had saturated, and to close little or none of the gap on factuality and reasoning benchmarks: the students learned the teacher's register — the formatting, the hedging, the confident opening sentence — and raters rewarded that from the first few thousand examples. Capability stayed roughly where the base model had left it.

The honest reading is not that imitation is worthless but that it does something narrower than it appeared. A small, well-chosen supervised set surfaces behaviour the pretrained model already had, which is the superficial alignment hypothesis that LIMA later tested with a thousand examples. It does not install knowledge or reasoning that pretraining failed to produce.

Three things. The data came from a competitor's model in breach of its terms, which made the whole lineage legally awkward and seeded the open corpora with synthetic teacher output that later models trained on in turn. The student inherits the teacher's errors and adds its own; Stanford withdrew the Alpaca demo partly over hallucination.

Most importantly, supervised imitation carries no preference signal. It can only say what a good answer looks like, never that one acceptable answer is better than another, and it has no way to express a dispreferred response at all. Recovering that ordering without InstructGPT's machinery is the problem DPO went after.

refs.t: Self-Instruct: Aligning Language Models with Self-Generated Instructions
The False Promise of Imitating Proprietary LLMs

llama2.lead: Llama 2 closed the gap the first release left open: a commercially licensed model shipped with its chat and safety pipeline rather than as a bare pretrained checkpoint. Its paper is the most detailed public account yet of an industrial RLHF programme — two separate reward models, five rounds of iteration, and a frank treatment of the conflict between being helpful and being safe that Anthropic had first documented. Llama 3 then scaled the pretraining data by an order of magnitude and quietly replaced PPO.

blocks.b:
Helpfulness and safety pull against each other, and a single reward model trained on both learns a compromise that satisfies neither. Llama 2 fits two, on binary comparisons annotated with a margin recording how strongly the preference was held, and combines them at optimisation time.

The process is iterative. Five successive versions were trained, each round collecting fresh preference data on the outputs of the current policy — because **a reward model goes stale as soon as the policy drifts off the distribution it was fitted on**, and a policy optimised against a stale reward will find its errors. Rejection sampling, drawing several completions and fine-tuning on the highest-scoring, was used alongside PPO, with the largest model's selections distilled into the smaller ones.

blocks.h: Quality over quantity, and Ghost Attention
blocks.b:
For supervised fine-tuning they found a few tens of thousands of carefully written demonstrations beat much larger bought-in instruction sets, and stopped purchasing data once the annotators' own work was outperforming it.

Ghost Attention addressed a specific failure: a system instruction such as a persona or a language constraint is honoured for a turn or two and then forgotten. The fix is a training-data trick rather than an architectural one. Take a sampled dialogue, prepend the instruction synthetically to every user turn, fine-tune with the loss zeroed on all but the final response, and the model learns to keep attending to the original instruction. Crude, and effective.

Llama 3 kept the shape and moved the numbers: roughly 15T pretraining tokens, a 128k-entry tokenizer, grouped-query attention at every size including the 8B, and context extended in stages to 128k. The 405B model followed.

Two decisions are worth naming. The architecture stayed dense despite Mixtral's showing, on the stated grounds of training stability at that scale. And post-training dropped PPO: the pipeline became supervised fine-tuning, rejection sampling, then DPO. Having the flagship open model settle on the simpler objective did more for its adoption than the original paper did.

The training data is undisclosed, so nothing about the pretraining is reproducible; what is released is a result, not a method. The licence carries an acceptable-use policy and a clause excluding the very largest deployments, which keeps it outside any standard open-source definition.

The safety alignment is also shallower than the effort suggests. Fine-tuning on a few hundred adversarial examples has been shown to strip refusal behaviour from these models cheaply, and that is not a bug in the RLHF so much as a consequence of the release model: once the parameters are public, no post-training procedure retains control over the behaviour. Alignment that survives an open release remains unsolved.

dpo.lead: DPO removes both the reward model and the reinforcement learning from RLHF while optimising the same objective. The observation is that the KL-constrained reward-maximisation problem has a closed-form solution, so the reward can be written as a function of the optimal policy; substitute that expression back into the preference likelihood and what is left is a binary classification loss that trains the language model directly on pairs.

blocks.b:
InstructGPT's procedure has three stages: supervised fine-tuning, fitting a reward model to pairwise human preferences, then PPO against that reward with a KL penalty holding the policy near its starting point.

The cost is not only conceptual. Training needs the policy, a frozen reference, the reward model and a value head in memory at once, with sampling from the policy inside the loop. The result is sensitive to the KL coefficient, to value-function initialisation and to batch composition, and reward hacking — the policy finding regions where the learned reward is high and the true preference is not — is the normal failure rather than the exceptional one. Few groups outside the large labs got it to work reliably.

blocks.h: The reward was already in the policy
blocks.b:
The KL-constrained objective $\max_{\pi} \mathbb{E}[r(x,y)] - \beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi \| \pi_{\mathrm{ref}})$ has a known optimum, an exponential tilt of the reference policy:

$\pi_r(y \mid x) = \tfrac{1}{Z(x)}\, \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x) \exp\!\left(\tfrac{1}{\beta} r(x,y)\right)$

Rearranged, $r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_r(y|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)} + \beta \log Z(x)$. Put this into the Bradley–Terry likelihood, which depends only on the difference of two rewards for the same prompt, and **the intractable partition function $Z(x)$ cancels**. What remains is

$-\log \sigma\!\left(\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w|x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l|x)}\right)$

for a preferred $y_w$ and dispreferred $y_l$. The gradient is weighted by how badly the implicit reward currently ranks the pair, so correctly ordered examples contribute little. Only forward passes through two frozen-and-trained models are needed, and $\beta$ inherits the role of the KL coefficient.

DPO sees a fixed set of pairs, usually generated by some other model. It can re-rank what it is shown and nothing else, and the implicit reward is unconstrained wherever the dataset has no support — so the optimisation is free to move probability mass onto responses no annotator ever judged.

The characteristic empirical symptom is that the log-probability of the preferred response often falls during training alongside the dispreferred one; only their margin is in the loss. Mass displaced from both can land somewhere neither was intended. Length bias is the other reliable one: longer completions tend to win comparisons, and nothing in the objective corrects for it.

IPO identified a specific pathology: when preferences in the data are deterministic, the Bradley–Terry likelihood is maximised by driving the margin to infinity, at which point the KL term no longer binds; replacing the log-sigmoid with a squared loss to a finite target margin fixes it. KTO drops the pairing requirement to learn from single thumbs-up or thumbs-down signals. ORPO folds the preference term into supervised fine-tuning and discards the reference model; SimPO normalises by length and does the same.

Iterative and online DPO restore the on-policy sampling that the derivation had removed, which is the honest admission that exploration was doing real work. GRPO went further back toward RL, keeping sampling but discarding the value network.

cot.lead: Chain-of-thought prompting changes nothing about the model. It adds worked intermediate steps to the handful of exemplars in the prompt, so the model imitates the working before committing to an answer — which on grade-school word problems took PaLM 540B from under a fifth correct to well over half. The gain appeared only in the largest models, making this the standard example of an ability that scale unlocks rather than one that training installs.

blocks.h: What one forward pass cannot do
blocks.b:
Few-shot prompting as GPT-3 established it puts the answer immediately after the question, so every step of a multi-step problem has to be completed inside one fixed-depth pass over a handful of answer tokens. Arithmetic word problems were where this bit hardest: on GSM8K the curve against model size was close to flat, and the largest models were not obviously better than much smaller ones at problems a child solves with a pencil.

The alternatives all required supervision — rationale-annotated training sets, or a verifier trained on sampled solutions to rerank them — collected per task. Chain-of-thought asked a cheaper question: whether the ability was already latent and had simply never been requested.

blocks.h: Eight exemplars with the working shown
blocks.b:
The method is the prompt. Each exemplar carries a question, a few sentences of ordinary reasoning, and only then the answer; the test question follows with nothing after it and the model continues in kind. No gradients, no annotation beyond the exemplars, no change to decoding.

Why it helps is mechanical rather than mystical. Generated tokens are fed back as input, so writing the working converts a problem that would need depth into one that needs length: the number of sequential operations available is no longer bounded by the layer count. It also makes failure legible. A wrong chain usually shows where the model went astray, which a bare wrong number cannot.

blocks.h: An ability only large models had
blocks.b:
The scaling behaviour is the paper's most-cited finding and its most awkward. Below roughly $10^{10}$ parameters the prompt produced fluent chains that were arithmetically wrong, often scoring worse than answering directly; the gains arrived with the largest models of the day and were largest on the hardest problems. Wei et al. called this emergence.

Schaeffer et al. later argued that much of the emergence literature is an artefact of discontinuous metrics — exact match on a final answer either fires or does not — and that smoother measures show continuous improvement. Either reading leaves the practical consequence intact: the prompt does not create the capability, so a model that cannot execute the steps will not learn to by being asked politely.

Variants followed within months. Kojima et al. recovered much of the gain with no exemplars at all, by appending an instruction to think step by step; self-consistency sampled many chains and took the majority answer, buying close to eighteen points on GSM8K for forty times the sampling compute. Both are still prompting.

Two problems went untouched. The written chain need not be the computation that produced the answer — Turpin et al. showed models swayed by biasing features their explanations never mention, so a plausible trace is not evidence of a faithful one. And elicitation has a ceiling set by the base model. Raising it meant putting the chain into the weights: STaR bootstrapped rationales from the model's own correct answers, and o1 and R1 trained them with reinforcement learning against graded outcomes.

o1.lead: o1 moved the chain of thought out of the prompt and into the weights: reinforcement learning on problems with checkable answers taught the model to deliberate at length, privately, before replying. Accuracy then rose with the amount of reinforcement learning done during training and, separately, with how long the model was allowed to think per question — the first widely visible demonstration that inference compute is a scaling axis of its own.

blocks.b:
By 2024 each further order of magnitude of pretraining was buying less on reasoning benchmarks than the one before it, and the supply of high-quality text is not unbounded. Meanwhile a separate line of work kept showing that spending more compute per question paid: sampling many candidate solutions and reranking them with a trained verifier, grading a solution step by step with a process reward model rather than only at the end, and searching over drafts.

Every one of those is a scaffold bolted around a fixed model, tuned per deployment. The wager behind o1 was that the scaffold could be folded into the model itself, so that the deliberation is generated rather than orchestrated.

OpenAI described the shape of the method and withheld the method: large-scale reinforcement learning in which the chain of thought is the object being optimised rather than the answer alone. What the reward is computed from was never stated — outcome correctness is the usual assumption, though OpenAI's own earlier work made the case for grading each step. What the published evaluations show is behaviour — the model decomposes a problem, notices its own mistake and backs out of it, abandons an approach that stalls and tries another — and that these strengthen as training compute grows rather than being written in by hand.

Because the behaviour now lives in the weights it needs no exemplars and survives on problems unlike anything a prompt could carry. The absence of published detail is not incidental here: it is the gap the open replications of 2025 were written against.

The gains concentrated sharply in domains with checkable answers. On the 2024 AIME papers GPT-4o solved roughly one problem in eight, while o1 solved around three-quarters at a single attempt and more when several samples were aggregated. It placed near the top decile of rated Codeforces competitors and, on the GPQA diamond set of graduate-level science questions, exceeded the score of human experts holding doctorates in the field.

On tasks with no right answer the picture was flat: raters preferred o1 on reasoning-heavy prompts and not on personal writing or editing. That asymmetry is the method showing through. An automatic grader is what makes a reward signal, and where no cheap grader exists there is nothing to reinforce.

blocks.h: Hidden tokens, and a running meter
blocks.b:
The raw chain is not shown. The stated reason is that a chain kept out of view need not be trained for policy compliance, and an unpoliced chain is a more honest thing to monitor for deception; users see a summary instead. The cost falls on them: reasoning tokens are billed and consume the context window while remaining unauditable, so neither the derivation nor the invoice can be checked.

Price and latency also became variable per question, and the model spends conspicuously on trivial ones. Two lines of work followed directly. One tries to control the thinking budget explicitly rather than leaving it to the policy; the other reconstructs the training recipe in the open, which is where DeepSeek-R1 arrives.

r1.lead: DeepSeek-R1 published what o1 had only demonstrated. Its precursor R1-Zero was trained by reinforcement learning directly on a base model with no supervised reasoning traces whatsoever, rewarded only by an automatic check of the final answer and a check that the working sat inside the right tags. The weights and the recipe were released under an MIT licence, and the failure modes were reported alongside the results.

blocks.b:
o1 established that reinforcement learning on chains of thought works and said almost nothing about how it was done. Replication attempts spread across tree search over reasoning steps, process reward models grading each intermediate line, and distillation from an existing reasoning model.

DeepSeek's paper is unusually explicit about trying two of these and abandoning them. Process rewards proved hard to define automatically at the step level, expensive to keep retraining, and — the decisive objection — vulnerable to reward hacking once a policy optimised against them at scale. Tree search foundered on the branching factor of token-level generation, where the moves are not a small discrete set. What remained was the crudest signal available, applied to the whole answer.

Two rewards, both computed by a program. An accuracy reward checks the final answer: a boxed result against the key for mathematics, a compiler and test suite for code. A format reward requires the reasoning to appear between `<think>` tags. No learned reward model appears in the reasoning stage at all, precisely because a learned grader is what gets gamed.

The optimiser is GRPO, which drops the value network. For each prompt it samples a group of $G$ answers, scores them, and uses the group as its own baseline:

$$A_i=\frac{r_i-\mathrm{mean}(r_1,\dots,r_G)}{\mathrm{std}(r_1,\dots,r_G)}$$

where $r_i$ is the reward of the $i$-th sample and $A_i$ its advantage in a clipped PPO-style update with a KL penalty back to the reference policy. Dropping the critic removes a second model-sized set of weights from memory.

blocks.h: What emerged, and how it read
blocks.b:
Left to optimise, R1-Zero grew its answers from hundreds of tokens to thousands over training, though nothing in the reward asked for length. Re-checking a step and backtracking appeared unprompted, and the paper records an inflection where the model interrupts a derivation to reconsider it. On the 2024 AIME problems R1-Zero reached around 71 per cent at a single attempt, and the high eighties with majority voting over samples.

The chains were also close to unusable: badly formatted, and mixing English and Chinese inside a single derivation. Pure outcome reinforcement optimises the answer and treats the reasoning as instrumental, so nothing prefers a legible chain to an illegible one that works.

blocks.h: What R1 added, and what it costs
blocks.b:
R1 fixes that in four stages, starting again from the base model rather than from R1-Zero's weights: a small cold-start supervised set of long, well-formed chains, some of it harvested from R1-Zero itself; reasoning RL with an added language-consistency reward; rejection sampling to build roughly 800k supervised examples covering reasoning and general tasks; and a final RL pass for helpfulness. The consistency reward was reported to cost a little accuracy — a trade recorded rather than buried.

Distilling those samples into Qwen and Llama models from 1.5B to 70B beat running the same RL directly on a small model: the capability is easier to transfer than to induce. What remains open: rewards exist only where an answer can be checked, leaving open-ended work untouched; long chains cost tokens; and few-shot prompting degrades this model rather than helping it.
